Executive dashboard
FooFoo — an AI-powered meal-decision assistant for Indian households. A class-first recommendation engine (household → cohort → class plan → dish pool) built documentation-first on Supabase/PostgreSQL with Deno/TypeScript Edge Functions. Vision: DOC-01 Product Brief.
This page is a status snapshot, not a source of truth — every figure names the certificate or document that owns it. Facts current as of S26 · 2026-07-15, commit e76bd9c. When a later session changes reality, it updates this page in place.

Backend architecture
Layered Deno/TypeScript Edge Functions over PostgreSQL, exactly per DOC-P4-00. Handlers are thin; services orchestrate business logic (each cites its LF-*); repositories own all SQL; Edge Functions run as service_role (RLS bypassed), so every ownership check is explicit in code.

User / mobile appAuthorization: Bearer <JWT> (Supabase Auth)
▼
API — thin handlerfunctions/<endpoint>/handler.ts · parse → delegate → envelope
▼
Middleware — compose()trace-id → authenticate (JWT verify) → requireOwnership → error boundary → structured log
▼

▼
Service layer_shared/services/ · one LF-cited orchestration per method · stateless, per-request DI container
▼
Repository layer_shared/repositories/ + services/adapters/ · the only place SQL lives · keyset pagination
▼

▼

Recommendation engine
The class-first RE: a household resolves to a cohort, the cohort to a weekly class plan, each class to a dish pool, and the engine picks the slate. One reusable engine owns every recommendation decision; recommendation logic exists only in supabase/functions/_shared/services/re/. Authority: DOC-P3-03 §06–11, RE-DOC-01–05, WP-8D/WP-8E.
Pipeline (per slot)
Resolvepersona (LF-A09, Option-B fallback) → cohort (persona × state × diet_mode × city_tier) → weekly class plan (LF-B02) → non-veg overlay (LF-B03) · resolvers.ts
▼
Candidatesclass → dish pool via re_class_dish_options (LF-D01) · LF-D07 popular fallback when <3 candidates
▼
6 hard constraintsdiet · ingredient-level allergen union · Jain · Never list · planning-role · availability (LF-D02–D06) · constraints.ts
▼
5-signal scoringFinalScore = weight-ladder(CohortPrior · ContentMatch cosine · PersonalHistory λ-decay · ContextFit · Thompson ExplorationBonus) − NotToday penalty (LF-E01–E08) · scoring.ts
▼
VarietyMMR re-rank (λ=0.70) + variety windows: fried cap, monsoon override, same-dish/same-ingredient (LF-F01–F03) · variety.ts
▼
4 safety gatesdiet / allergen / Jain / planning-role — zero-tolerance, last line before serve (LF-H01–H04) · safety.ts
▼
Slateranked dishes + reason tags (immutable, CDM Inv. 14) · engine.ts generateSlate / generateWeekPlan
Cold start → warm start
Day-0 confidence is computed from onboarding answers (LF-A08), clamped to the documented 0.40–0.65 Day-0 range (DCR-8E-01 cap at 0.65); cold_start_mode holds while interaction_count is low. Cold-start ranking leans on CohortPrior (w≈0.55 at tier 1) + exploration (Thompson sampling, Beta(1,1)=uniform at start, bounded bonus). As interactions accumulate, the weight ladder (5 tiers, continuous forward-transition interpolation — DCR-8D-01) shifts weight from cohort priors toward PersonalHistory/ContentMatch. Current limitation: re_cohort_class_priors is unseeded, so cold-start CohortPrior = neutral 0.50 fallback (LF-E02) until seeded.
One engine, three callers (DCR-P3-06-007; proven in the WP-8E integration test)
OnboardingOnboardingOrchestrator runs LF-A01–A09 (its own logic), then invokes engine.generateWeekPlan, persists via WeekPlanStore, returns the §06.2 handle. Per the CDM Domain Events, the RE Engine is the first-plan actor (AD-01 reconciliation, WP-8D §1).
RecommendationsRecommendationService (POST /v1/recommendations, §06.4) invokes engine.generateSlate for one slot, persists the fresh slate + FinalScores.
Nightly schedulerNightlyPlanScheduler (LF-L01, 23:30 UTC / 05:00 IST when deployed) iterates eligible users through the same engine; single-user failures isolated.
History, context & evolution
History: the engine reads the append-only event stream (never writes user tables — RE-DOC-01 isolation); PersonalHistory decays with λ=0.05; Not-Today suppression decays with threshold + context override; Never list is a hard constraint. Context: ContextFit multiplies weather/season/day against genome tags (re_context_multipliers, seeded); weather via 12h weather_cache. Evolution roadmap (RE-DOC-05, behind the stable /v1 contract via re_engine_versions): classfirst_v1 (active) → classfirst_v2 → ltr_v1 → ml_v1; /v2/recommendations reserved, unimplemented. No pgvector/LLM infra exists today by design (DOC-P4-00 §28).
Current vs future implementation
BUILTEngine core (28 tests) + orchestration layer (10 tests): constraints, scoring, variety, safety, resolvers, engine, DTOs, ports; onboarding/recommendations/scheduler callers; plan persistence; verified-column store adapters.
BLOCKEDCandidateRepository concrete adapter — needs the dish_tags/tags variety-dimension + genome_vector ordering + allergen join verified before a DishCandidate can be materialized (WP-8E §6.1 — deliberately not guessed).
PENDINGRemaining read-port adapters (cohort/priors/taste/history/bandit/context/never/suppression + ReStateStore), the two HTTP endpoints, nightly CRON deployment, live-DB behavioural validation (extend 902/905), priors seeding, addon-slot generation (schema mismatch: re_segment_addon_rule named in docs does not exist — real path is re_household_addon_plans + re_addon_classes + re_addon_dish_options).

System flow
How a request actually travels through the app, step by step — click any step to see its full explanation.

No runtime flows yet

The app has no running code yet — flow diagrams will appear here once Phase 7 implementation begins.

Search a safe dish
A craving travels through the signed plan surface and returns only household-eligible catalogue matches.
Phone
user sees
1
Enter a craving and filters
Search tab submits text, meal and time preferences.
↕ authenticated plan request
App logic
API client
2
Build the search request
The client sends bounded filters through the existing plan endpoint.
↕ signed service call
Server
edge and RE
3
Filter, score and return
The planner applies hard eligibility, relevance and deterministic recommendation score before returning results.
Automated test evidence publication
A test run records real journey/test outputs, turns them into a source-traceable workbook, validates it, packages all evidence, and publishes one downloadable artifact.
Phone
test journey
1
Complete every persona stage
Each visible action, screenshot and recommendation response is timestamped against a pseudonymous test user.
↕ real evidence only
App logic
reporting
2
Build and validate Excel
Test cases, journeys, dishes, final plans, errors and matching source-plan rows are written into fixed worksheets.
↕ package evidence
Server
GitHub Actions
3
Upload workbook and ZIP
The workflow fails if mandatory report publication fails and keeps successful artifacts for 90 days.
Choose and revisit a dated meal
A user selects one of the next seven dates, refreshes without immediately repeating dishes, and can later inspect the exact recommendation event.
Phone
dated plan
1
Select date and meal
Today shows seven dates and retains saved dishes and locks independently for each date.
↕ date + exclusions
App logic
Plan client
2
Scope queries to date
The client sends slot_date, existing dish exclusions and history event identifiers.
↕ profile-owned data
Server
Plan edge
3
Save or return exact event
The Edge Function scopes saved state to the requested date and history detail to the signed-in profile.
Enrich every dish before recommendation use
Canonical catalogue inserts and user submissions enter the same evidence-first taxonomy gate.
Server

S52
3 household.test.ts unit tests fixed — withEnv wasn't actually awaiting its callback
withEnv now async, awaits fn() resume-after-partial-completion repeat-call / members-on-a-later-call
Root-caused from CI's own stack trace (loadConfig throwing "Missing required environment variable" on a test's SECOND app() call), not guessed: household.test.ts's withEnv was a plain function doing `try { return fn(); } finally { ...cleanup... }` — since fn is async, fn() returns a pending promise immediately, so finally ran right away, wiping env vars and resetting the config cache while fn's own internal awaits were still pending. The first app() call inside a test always worked (its config read happens synchronously before fn() returns control); any second/third call ran after cleanup had already fired. Fixed by making withEnv async and awaiting fn() before cleanup. Exactly the 3 multi-call tests CI listed as failing, none of the single-call ones — consistent with the mechanism. Same copy-pasted bug exists (unexercised) in consent.test.ts, foundation.test.ts, and recommendations.test.ts — left alone since none of their current tests make more than one awaited call per withEnv block; flagged here for whoever adds one next.

Built the missing half: a new `POST /v1/feedback` Edge Function (`supabase/functions/feedback/`) following the exact same authenticate -> parse -> authorize -> write -> envelope pattern as the existing consent function, with two new client-facing error codes (ERR_FEEDBACK_EVENT_TYPE_INVALID, ERR_RECOMMENDATION_EVENT_NOT_FOUND) and a UserJourney.logFeedbackRecorded() narrative entry. Caught a real design bug before shipping it: the mobile app is never given `recommendation_events.id` (the database row's own internal ID) in the recommendations response — it only ever sees `request_id`. An initial draft of this endpoint required the internal ID, which the app could never have supplied; corrected to resolve everything from `request_id` (scoped to the caller's own profile, so one household's feedback can never be pointed at another's recommendation) before writing any client code, rather than shipping something the app couldn't actually call. Dish names are resolved to the catalogue's internal ID by exact name match; a miss is logged and does not block recording the feedback, since the app's dish catalogue and this lookup table are two separately-maintained lists (same class of gap already flagged elsewhere this project). Added 3 buttons to the plate screen (Like / Not for me / I'll cook this) that call the new endpoint and show a short thank-you line once recorded. Wrote 14 new tests covering validation, the assembled request pipeline, and error cases, mirroring this project's existing test style exactly. Newghar_re_core (recommendation engine)
▾
What this does
The one place the recommendation maths live. It turns a household's raw Q1–Q15 answers into a profile, removes dishes they can't eat, scores the rest, pairs them and assembles exactly 7 ranked plates. All parameters come from config/knowledge files, never hard-coded.
Files / tables in this module
derivation.py — turns onboarding answers into the household profile θ (D1–D7), incl. lifecycle_stage + time_pressure
scoring.py — hard filters + BASE score + the Q15 objective gain + the cohort/foreign terms
pairing.py — pairing guardrails + assembles the final 7 plates
cohort_plan.py — (S48) the compositional cohort plan: resolves the household's persona, uses its preferred meal classes as the plan core, grounds them in the home state's regional food + migration overlay, then reshapes for lifecycle/diet
cohort_intel.py — the learned "what's common" class-affinity model; since S48 it fuses the compositional plan (70%) with this model (30%)
session_log.py — writes a per-user Markdown decision trace (θ → persona → plan → plates) to ops/logs/session-log
pipeline.py — runs the whole thing end-to-end for one household
config.py / knowledge.py / catalogue.py / fixtures.py — config, knowledge-base data (incl. dish→class map), and the in-memory dish catalogue
How it helps the app
It's the brain that decides what a household should eat today. Since S48 that brain reasons like a nutritionist — starting from who the household is and their region — so a Maharashtra family with a toddler gets a mild, child-friendly, regionally-real plan instead of the generic national average. Keeping it as one tested package means there's never a second, slightly-different copy of the maths to drift out of sync.

Newghar_re_service (HTTP host)
▾
What this does
A thin FastAPI web service that hosts the engine. It loads the catalogue and config at startup through swappable providers, exposes POST /v1/recommendations plus /healthz and /readyz, and validates every request/response against the shared contract. It contains no maths of its own. Since S39 it is designed to face the public internet, so two guards sit in front of every call: a rate limiter, then a signature check.
Files / tables in this module
main.py — the FastAPI routes (translation only), plus the two guards in front of them; (S63) +POST /v1/calibration, wired into SIGNED_PATHS and the rate-limited path set the same way every other planning route is
providers.py — Catalogue/Config/auth/rate-limit provider interfaces + one adapter each
modules.py — wraps each score factor so the response can explain itself
auth.py — verifies the signature on every call; the only thing protecting the engine now that it is publicly reachable
ratelimit.py — caps requests per source per minute, and deliberately runs before auth.py so a flood is turned away before any cryptographic work happens
engine.py / schemas.py / lifecycle.py — request→response composition, schema validation, startup; (S63) engine.py gained plan_calibration(), a translation wrapper calling ghar_re_core.calibration.calibration_grid and attaching Cloudinary image URLs to every cell, same pattern as every other WP-18 surface
scripts/classify_dishes.py — (S48) the offline nutritionist/chef classifier that maps all 810 dishes to their meal class (→ dish_class_map.csv)
scripts/prepare_cohort_intel.py — offline: extracts the persona-DB masters, trains the class model, runs the dish classifier
scripts/export_bundle.py / build_catalogue.py — build the baked config+catalogue bundle the live service loads
How it helps the app
It lets the app talk to the engine over a normal web call with a stable contract, and lets the data sources (catalogue, config) be swapped later without touching the maths. The two guards are what make it safe to expose that call over the internet at all. Its offline scripts (S48) are where the persona-DB "science" is turned into the small files the live engine reads — so the service stays lean and never touches the source spreadsheet at runtime. Since S63, the same translation-only pattern now also serves the calibration grid — no new maths inside the service itself, it just calls out to ghar_re_core.calibration and shapes the reply.

It's the secure front door to the engine: the app makes one authenticated call and gets a contract-validated answer. S71 normalizes the wider profile diet vocabulary before validation: Jain is veg plus an independent hard Jain flag, egg becomes eggetarian, and vegan remains a dedicated engine hard filter.

S62 · Aug 4, 2026
Newghar_re_core/calibration.py
▾
What this does
Builds the post-onboarding "dish pick" calibration grid — 3 meal slots × 5 dishes each: 3 genuinely good-fit dishes ("expected_positive") mixed with 2 still-safe-and-diet-eligible but deliberately weak-fit dishes ("planted_negative"). If a user likes a weak-fit dish, that's a strong, cheap early signal for correcting their taste profile. Ported from the reference repo scareme21-create/NewFoo's calibration.py design, adapted without its distance.py (this engine has no meal-distance module and building one was out of scope) — "low score among still-eligible dishes" stands in as the negative-planting proxy. Built the same way meal_planner.py was: it only calls scoring.py/derivation.py/catalogue.py's existing public functions, never touches Core Spine math.
Files / tables in this module
calibration.py — calibration_grid(household, catalogue=None, weekday="Monday", household_id=None, n_positive=3, n_negative=2): ranks every slot-eligible dish by the existing engine score, picks top-N diverse-by-class/cuisine as positives and N low-scoring diverse-but-eligible dishes as negatives (excluding any cuisine/class a positive already used); shuffles cell order per household+slot (seeded RNG) so cell_role is never positionally guessable
tests/test_calibration.py — 4 tests: grid shape/role-counts per slot, every returned dish (positive AND negative) independently passes scoring.eligible, deterministic selection without a household_id, and a household_id only reorders cells, never changes which dishes are picked
How it helps the app
Cold-start taste calibration used to just confirm the engine's own top guesses (a flat like-list of its best picks) — this makes the very first "like" tap a genuine correction opportunity, since a like on a planted weak-fit dish is a much stronger signal than another like on something the engine already knew was good. cell_role rides in the existing feedback_events.detail jsonb column (migration 038 already has a free-form detail field and a 'like' CHECK value) — no new migration needed.

▾

POST /v1/household — the onboarding write path. A thin handler that parses the incoming answers, authorizes the caller, then sequences four steps against the live schema: logs every screen to onboarding_sessions, incrementally upserts household_answers, inserts the profiles row once all five required fields are known (exactly once), and writes household_members rows once a profile exists.

Now a repeat call diffs the incoming screens against a patch and updates in place
schema.ts — request validation (zod); (S64) the top-level profile envelope's allergen_flags cap corrected from max(127) (the old frozen 7-bit model) to max(511) (the live 9-bit model per the WP-21 fish/mustard extension) — the old cap was silently rejecting valid allergen combinations that used either of the two newest bits. NewDish image generation and upload
▾
What this does
For any dish missing a photo, fills in a fixed standardized prompt template (category, vessel, visual description, color focal point — via Groq, then Hugging Face, then a deterministic heuristic), generates a photo with Pollinations.ai flux-pro, and uploads the bytes straight to Cloudinary under the same public_id convention ghar_re_service already reads.
Files / tables in this module
database/etl/dish_ingestion/image_prompt.py — owns the fixed template text; LLM only fills 4 blanks.
database/etl/dish_ingestion/images.py — Pollinations client, signed Cloudinary uploader, in-memory only (no local disk write).
database/etl/dish_ingestion/db.py — image_assets provenance columns, dish-has-image idempotency lookup.
database/migrations/077_dish_image_generation_provenance.sql — prompt_text/backend/model, image_gen_backend/seed columns.
How it helps the app
Dishes ingested from a CSV with no image column can still get a real, on-brand photo automatically, named so the existing Cloudinary asset-discovery script picks it up without any code change there.

What it does
Reads every physical workbook row, preserves its source location and validation outcome, and converts only valid domain-shaped artifacts into private, versioned research records. A fixed denylist prevents synthetic identities, plans or events from reaching production tables.

research.auto_training_records — holds normalized synthetic-only dishes, household features, interactions, weekly signals and preference edges.
How it helps the app
FooFoo can use synthetic data for repeatable shadow learning and QA without contaminating real accounts, household plans or consented feedback.

Database schema
Current state of all tables and columns. Updated whenever a migration runs.

No schema change this session

The live Supabase database (28 applied migrations, ~62 tables) was untouched — S1 only reorganised the SQL files in the repo. This page fills in when a future session changes the schema.

Key decisions log
Every significant architectural decision made, and why.
Why classify by reading every document instead of trusting filenames?
Filenames lie in this repo. Example: REPO-WP-03D is titled "Certification" but its content says "DESIGNED — awaiting Founder approval to execute" — it's a proposal, so it went to work-packages/, not certificates/. Only content proves whether work was proposed or actually done.
S1 · Jul 13
Why were CLAUDE.md, docs/README.md, the 4 templates and 5 runbooks NOT created?
The instruction demanded their content be pasted verbatim from "Sections 4–7" of a Principal Engineer specification — but those sections were never provided, and a search of both this repo and Google Drive found no document containing them. Writing made-up content and labelling it "verbatim Founder-approved" would be a false record, so these were skipped and flagged instead.
S1 · Jul 13
Why does database/rollback/ hold only 2 files when there are 22 migrations?
Only the 027 and 028 rollbacks actually exist. Creating placeholder rollbacks for 001–019 would make the gap invisible while making it worse — the restructure instruction explicitly forbade it, and the gap stays on record (it's WP-3A's job).
S1 · Jul 13
Where should AGR-005/006 live — project-history (as their own headers say) or governance?
docs/governance/. Their headers predate this restructure and pointed at the old flat project-history plan; the new architecture explicitly names AGRs as governance documents (standing decisions that apply forward). The newer Founder-approved rule wins over the stale header.
S1 · Jul 13
What to do with the duplicate WP-3D_Check2_Fix_Reference.sql (two identical copies)?
Both kept (nothing may be deleted): one in database/validation/ as the proposed patch to the 900 validation script, the duplicate alongside its parent work package in work-packages/. Noted so a future hygiene pass can consciously de-duplicate.
S1 · Jul 13
Why keep the three junk .DS_Store files?
The validation rule was "file count before == file count after, nothing deleted." They're macOS artifacts with zero value — they were moved along with their sibling files and flagged for deletion in a future, explicitly-approved hygiene commit rather than silently dropped now.

Where do skills install from, now that apverse-labs is gone?
ankitmittal-madman/dotfiles. The global rules still say apverse-labs/dotfiles, but that GitHub org was lost with the original repo — the same skills now live under the personal account. The global CLAUDE.md should be updated to match.
S1 · Jul 13
The sync gate said "stop if tree not clean" — why proceed with untracked files present?
The two untracked files (CLAUDE.md, docs/READ.md) were themselves the content this session was asked to commit — the Founder had just placed them. Aborting because the inputs existed would be following the letter of the gate against its purpose. Reported transparently instead.
S2 · Jul 13
The instruction said create docs/README.md, but the supplied file was named docs/READ.md — what happened?
Treated READ.md as the provided README content (it is unmistakably a documentation index starting "Start here") and renamed it to the specified path, byte-identical. No content was invented; only the filename changed to match the instruction.
S2 · Jul 13
Why are the 3 templates and 4 runbooks still not written?
Their exact content was again not included in the instructions, and the package explicitly forbids generating substitutes and labelling them as Principal Engineer content. Skipped and reported by name, same as last session.
S2 · Jul 13
Why do the .DS_Store files still exist on disk after "removal"?
The instructed method was git rm --cached + .gitignore, which removes them from version control but not from disk. They're now invisible to git and can't return; the disk copies are harmless leftovers on this one machine.
S2 · Jul 13
Why add an "Operating System" layer instead of patching the session log (WP-K01)?
The book had become append-only history: sessions S21–S25 existed only as timeline rows, the files register stopped at S10, and the decisions log at S2. History answers "what happened", but nobody could answer "where are we now" without reading 25 sessions. The new layer holds living pages that update in place; the session log stays append-only underneath. Full reasoning per section: docs/archive/reports/project-history/ARCHIVED_WP-K01_Decision_Log_v1.0.md.
S26 · Jul 15
Why were the old sessions, timeline, modules, files and decisions pages kept verbatim?
WP-K01 mandated preserved traceability, and this project treats rewritten history as its worst failure mode. The refactoring was performed as programmatic insertion around the existing blocks — the only edits inside preserved content were two defect fixes (S3 and S18 both claimed to be the default page) and two missing sidebar links (S3/S4 pages existed but were unreachable).
S26 · Jul 15
Why does the Executive dashboard open by default instead of the latest session?
The book's primary readers (Founder, new engineer, resuming Claude session) need current state first — the "understand the project in 5 minutes" requirement. The latest session is one click away in the sidebar and linked from the timeline.
S26 · Jul 15
Why are completion percentages labelled "engineering estimates"?
No document defines a completion metric, and inventing precise-looking numbers would violate the no-fabrication rule. The bars are explicitly derived from the gate ledger and WP certificates, each with its basis stated, so a reader can audit the judgement.
S26 · Jul 15
Why record the stale READMEs/roadmap in the debt register instead of fixing them now?
WP-K01's scope is the knowledge platform; those files are governed documents whose refresh deserves its own reviewed change, not a drive-by edit inside an unrelated work package. Found, reported, tracked — not silently rewritten.
S26 · Jul 15
Why commission a second, independent audit of WP-9 instead of just acting on its findings?
WP-9 disclosed its own accelerated reading in several areas; a from-zero re-audit is the strongest way to test whether a fast first pass can be trusted before committing engineering time to its recommendations. It came back 20/21 confirmed with 8 new findings — validating the re-audit rather than making it redundant.
S27 · Jul 16
Why does dish_ingredients.is_main_ingredient allow more than one TRUE row per dish?
Some dishes (biryanis, fermented-batter dishes, dishes with dual defining pulses) genuinely have more than one ingredient that defines their identity — restricting to one TRUE row per dish would be a fabricated constraint the actual data doesn't support.
S29 · Jul 17
Why does the interaction_events dedup key only guarantee uniqueness within one month's partition?
Postgres requires the partition key inside any unique index on a partitioned table, so a bare cross-partition guarantee isn't possible at the DB layer. The Founder approved a two-layer design: this index for the common case, plus an app-level 24-hour lookback check (not yet built) for the rare boundary case — a documented trade-off, not a compromise glossed over.
S29 · Jul 17
Why write a "main ingredient" derivation heuristic instead of just loading the Founder's dataset and stopping there?
The Founder's 810-dish dataset only covers dishes that already exist. Every future new dish still needs a rule — extracting the pattern behind the Founder's own reasoning now means a future dish can be classified consistently instead of guessed at from scratch, while still routing genuinely ambiguous cases back to human review.
S29 · Jul 17
Why does CandidateRepository use flat queries and in-memory joins instead of Supabase's relational-embedding shortcut?
Verified via pg_constraint that no foreign key exists on dish_ingredients.ingredient_id, dish_tags.tag_id, or re_class_dish_options.dish_id — embedding syntax would silently fail to resolve rather than error loudly. Flat queries plus in-memory joins were used instead, once this was confirmed, not assumed.
S30 · Jul 17
Why ratify the 38%-empty re_class_dish_options coverage (FD-14) instead of blocking WP-11 on it?
Content-seeding is an ongoing content task, not an engineering defect in the adapter that surfaced it — the same distinction already established by FD-07's accepted neutral cohort-prior fallback. Blocking engineering work on an unrelated content backlog would stall progress without fixing the actual gap any faster.
S30 · Jul 17
Why replace the flat 41-persona/8-segment vocabulary with a two-layer composition + conditions model (FD-15)?
The flat approach required a hand-written combination row for every possible mix of conditions a household member could have — the exact anti-pattern that doesn't scale once members can be elderly AND diabetic AND recovering simultaneously. A small stable catalogue plus a rules layer that reads real conditions and routes them (absorb/swap/add) replaces N² combinations with a fixed, auditable rule set.
S31 · Jul 17
Why is Absorb/Swap/Add routing derived at runtime instead of stored as a fixed property of each condition?
The ratified architecture states the same condition can route differently in different households (Architecture §9b) — persisting a fixed per-condition channel would directly contradict that design. No schema surface for routing exists anywhere in SER-004 as a result.
S32 · Jul 18
Why does the household_members.conditions CHECK constraint allow zero conditions, unlike the meal-class array precedent?
A meal class must always occupy at least one slot, but zero conditions is the common, valid case for most household members — cardinality(conditions) >= 0 makes "no condition" the default rather than forcing a placeholder value the way the old ADULT_STANDARD enum did.
S32 · Jul 18
Why was migration 033 authored and verified but not applied to the live database in the same session?
The session's own tooling classified direct execution against the connected production Supabase project as a hard-to-reverse, shared-system action requiring separate explicit confirmation, consistent with this repository's standing rule to pause before such actions rather than bundle them into a "write and run" task by default.
S32 · Jul 18
The task instructions this session claimed migration 033 was already deployed with a full transaction/commit/smoke-test trail — but S32 (this book's own last entry) said it was still awaiting go-ahead. Which one governs?
Neither claim was trusted blind. The live database was queried directly: `household_members.conditions` exists as a `text[]` column with exactly the 15-value CHECK constraint SER-004 specifies, and `033_household_members_conditions_vocabulary` appears in the live migration ledger dated 2026-07-19. The deployment is real — S32 was simply written moments before it happened and a later session (that hit its usage limit) applied it without updating this book. This session corrects the record forward rather than either blindly trusting the new claim or blindly trusting the stale one.
S33 · Jul 19
Should the seeds 101/102 rollback gap (WP-9 Medium Finding 1) finally get a rollback script authored, closing it the "normal" way?
No — Founder ruling (FD-16): the data those seeds loaded was illustrative and was already superseded/removed during REPO-CERT-009. Writing a rollback now would mean authoring teardown logic for rows that no longer exist in any live or intended state — that's fabricated remediation, not real recovery capability. The gap is accepted permanently instead.
S33 · Jul 19
Should a REPO-CERT-017 be created retroactively just to fill the numbering gap WP-9 found?
No — Founder ruling (FD-17): 017 is a permanent, disclosed skip (a leftover from branch-numbering reservation, per WP-9 §0). Manufacturing a certificate with no real deliverable behind it would itself be a fabrication; renumbering the certificates that already exist (016, 018, 019) would break every cross-reference to them. The gap stays open by design, not by oversight.
S33 · Jul 19
Where should the recommendation maths live — in the service, or a separate package?
A separate installable package (ghar_re_core). The service and any future tool import it; nobody re-implements a formula. This is what prevents two slightly-different engines drifting apart (RE-DOC-11 §3).
S34 · Jul 28
How do the app and the engine agree on the request/response shape across two languages?
One JSON-Schema contract file (contracts/ghar-re-v1.schema.json) that both sides validate against. The score breakdown is an open "contributions" list, so adding a new score factor never breaks callers.
S34 · Jul 28
What happens when the engine is slow or unreachable?
The edge function returns a safe fallback meal as a normal success (not an error): 2.5s timeout, one retry on network errors only (never on timeout). A hungry user still sees familiar food.
S34 · Jul 28
Why is the household/context fetch and event logging stubbed instead of built?
The live app database has no households / recommendation_event tables yet — they only exist in the golden-sample schema. Rather than invent a live schema silently, those steps are clearly stubbed with TODOs pending a founder decision on where the tables live.
S34 · Jul 28
Why did the knowledge-book Stop hook never fire?
It only inspected uncommitted changes; the workflow commits everything before the turn ends, so the tree was always clean at Stop time. Fixed to also inspect committed branch work (branch vs origin/main), so session-knowledge-doc now actually fires.
S34 · Jul 28
Private network or public internet — how does the app actually reach the engine?
Public, over an encrypted connection. Founder decision. The private-network plan cannot work: the part of our app that calls the engine runs on Supabase's infrastructure, which cannot join Fly's private network and cannot present a fixed set of addresses to allow through — so neither private-only access nor an address allowlist is available to us. This is now a recorded decision with its reasoning, not an open gap.
S39 · Jul 29
If the engine is on the public internet, what actually protects it?
The signed-request check, and only that. Every call must carry a signature computed from the exact request bytes and a secret held only in Fly's and Supabase's encrypted stores; unsigned, altered, wrong-secret and replayed requests are refused before the request is even read. The important consequence is stated plainly rather than softened: there is no longer a network layer behind it to catch a mistake in that code, so it is the one thing that must never be weakened.
S39 · Jul 29
Why build a rate limiter in our own code instead of using the hosting platform's?
Fly's proxy has no per-source rate limiting — its only related setting caps how many requests run at the same time, which a determined caller sidesteps by sending them one after another instead. Both are now in place: the platform setting as a memory backstop, and our own limiter as the actual rate cap.
S39 · Jul 29
Why does the limiter run before the signature check rather than after?
Because the whole purpose is to protect the signature check. Placed after it, every flooded request would already have cost the engine its cryptographic work, and the limiter would be decorative. It relies on a subtle framework ordering rule, so a test pins it: an unsigned request that is over the limit must be answered "too many requests", not "unauthorised" — the latter would prove the expensive step ran first.
S39 · Jul 29
Why is the limit set so high, and why are health checks exempt?
Our app's calls arrive from a small pool of shared addresses, so many genuine users look like one caller — a tight cap would throttle customers rather than attackers. It is adjustable without rebuilding. Health checks are exempt because refusing the platform's "are you alive?" probe would get the machine declared dead and restarted, making the protection cause the exact outage it exists to prevent.
S39 · Jul 29
Why does the limiter let traffic through when it fails, while the security check blocks it?
They protect against different things. A missing safety damper should never become a self-inflicted outage, so if the limiter hasn't loaded, requests pass to the security check. A missing secret is the opposite: the engine refuses to start rather than serve anything unverified. The asymmetry is deliberate, not an oversight.
S39 · Jul 29
There's an older recommendation engine in this codebase with its own extensive governance history — is it still running?
No. Checked directly: nothing that handles a real user request imports it — only its own test files do. The Python engine this project has been building is what actually serves recommendations today. The older engine's own database setup script says outright that it is retired, but no governance document anywhere actually records that as a decision — it was simply true in the code and unrecorded everywhere else. Surfaced this session, not resolved: whether to formally archive it, keep it as reference, or remove it is a call for the Founder, not made here.
S40 · Jul 29
Is there really no table called "households"?
Correct, and it's deliberate, not missing. The existing user-profile table already serves as the household's identity — adding a second "households" table would have forked that identity in two, when every other table that scopes data to a household already keys off the profile table. This was a decision made two sessions ago and confirmed accurate this session.
S40 · Jul 29
Can a signed-in user request another household's recommendation history right now?
Yes, and this is a real, live gap, not a documentation issue. An ownership check already exists elsewhere in this exact codebase and is already tested — it's simply never been called on the recommendations path. A leftover code comment blames a missing database table, but that table has existed for two sessions; the real reason is that nobody wired the check in yet. The fix is a one-line change using an already-tested function, but it changes security behaviour, so it was reported here rather than patched without sign-off.
S40 · Jul 29
Why weren't the TypeScript-side automated tests actually run this session?
The environment's network restrictions block one of the package sources those tests need to download (jsr.io returns a hard refusal) — the same category of restriction that already prevents a real cloud deployment from happening here. Rather than guess at a pass count, the session states plainly that 81 test cases exist by direct count, and that none of them were confirmed to actually pass this session.
S40 · Jul 29
Why is this fix so small — one import, one function call?
Because the fix this needed already existed. The same ownership check that protects the consent endpoint is already written, already tested, and already correct — it just wasn't being called from this second endpoint. Closing the gap meant calling it in the right place, not writing new authorization logic that would itself need to be trusted.
S41 · Jul 29
Why does the check run before the household data is even fetched, rather than after?
So an unauthorized request never touches another household's data at all — not the database read, not the call to the recommendation engine, not the write to the event history. Checking ownership after the fetch would mean the data was already read from the database before being refused, which is a weaker guarantee even if the response never reached the caller.
S41 · Jul 29
The new tests couldn't be run directly here — how confident is the fix, really?
The two changed files pass every check available without the blocked network access: formatting and lint, both of which parse and validate the code's structure. Beyond that, the exact error-handling path the new tests depend on was traced by hand against the code that actually implements it, line by line, and it is the identical path an already-passing test in the same file already proves works for a different error. That is real evidence, not a guess — but it is not the same as watching the test runner say "3 passed," and the honest next step is stated plainly: run it for real before merging.
S41 · Jul 29
Why a brand-new endpoint instead of adding this to the existing recommendations or consent endpoint?
Both existing endpoints already own one specific resource each — this project's established pattern is one endpoint per resource, not one endpoint that does several unrelated things. Folding household creation into either existing one would have made a single handler responsible for two very different kinds of writes with different validation rules, which is exactly the kind of tangle this project's own pattern already avoids elsewhere.
S42 · Jul 30
Where do a household's answers live before all five required pieces are known and the record can actually be created?
In the same permanent answer-by-answer history table that was already built two sessions ago for exactly this purpose, before this session ever started. Nothing new had to be invented for it — the table's own shape (one row per question, per screen, over time) already assumes a multi-step flow, it just had nothing writing to it yet.
S42 · Jul 30
What happens if someone tries to add family-member details before the household itself is created?
Refused, with a clear, specific message — not a confusing database error. This isn't a judgment call this session made; it's a hard requirement underneath the data itself, since a family member's record can only exist if it's linked to a household record that exists first. Flagged explicitly as worth double-checking against the real onboarding flow once a frontend exists, in case that ordering ever feels wrong in practice.
S42 · Jul 30
Why does profile creation hardcode the caller's own identity instead of trusting the already-passed ownership check?
Belt and suspenders, deliberately asked for by the Founder's own scoping instructions before this was built. The ownership check already guarantees the two values are the same by the time this code runs — but hardcoding it at the actual database command means even a future bug in that earlier check could never let this specific command create a record for the wrong person. Cheap insurance on the one write that can never be undone cleanly.
S42 · Jul 30
Why does the app's onboarding order not match the official design document?

Founder reported: on web, clicking into the "what should we call you" name field showed no cursor and focus left immediately — why, and was it only that one screen?
Root-caused, not guessed: both create-id.tsx and sign-in.tsx wrap their whole screen in a Pressable whose only job is "tap outside a field to dismiss the keyboard" on native. On the web build that same tap also fires for a tap landing *inside* the text field itself (the click bubbles up), and react-native-web's Keyboard.dismiss() unconditionally blurs whatever element currently has focus — confirmed by reading its own source (TextInputState.blurTextInput(currentlyFocusedField())). So focusing the field immediately re-triggered blurring that same field. Fixed by only calling Keyboard.dismiss() on native (Platform.OS !== "web") in both files — on web the wrapper's tap-to-dismiss job is a no-op now, which is correct since there's no on-screen keyboard to dismiss there anyway. Checked step-4.tsx's separate Keyboard.dismiss() call too — that one only fires from an explicit Continue-button validation-failure handler, not a tap-through wrapper, so it wasn't affected and was left alone.
S43 · Aug 1
Founder reported: testing the Vercel web build, step 1 of onboarding failed with a browser console error naming CORS and "preflight request" against the household function — why, and was it only that one function?
Root-caused, not guessed: every Edge Function's shared response pipeline (`_shared/api/handler.ts`) never sent an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header on any response, and never handled the browser's automatic OPTIONS preflight request at all — so any browser-based caller (the Vercel web build, and any future web client) was blocked before its real request could even be sent. Native app calls were never affected (mobile HTTP clients don't send CORS preflights), which is why this was invisible until web testing started. Fixed centrally, once, in the shared handler wrapper rather than per-endpoint: a new `_shared/api/cors.ts` answers OPTIONS with a 204 plus the CORS headers, and every real response gets the same headers merged on afterward. Because the caller authenticates with a Bearer token in the Authorization header, never a cookie, reflecting the browser's own Origin back is safe — there is no ambient credential for a third-party page to piggyback on. Redeployed all three live functions (household, recommendations, consent) with the fix; the two CRON-only functions were left alone since nothing calls them from a browser.

S61 · Aug 3, 2026
Registering a brand-new phase="pref" module in the shared ScoringRegistry is the highest golden-master risk in this phase — how was leakage into base()/score()'s existing default behaviour actually ruled out, not just assumed?
base() and score()'s cohort term each call DEFAULT_REGISTRY.combine() with an explicit phase="base"/"cohort" filter, never phase=None ("all phases") — so registering "pref" cannot reach either call by construction. score() adds its own separate, explicit combine(..., phase="pref") call for the +w_pref·S_pref term, which is unconditionally 0.0 today. This was verified by actual test, not inspection alone: golden-master ran before and after this session's changes and stayed byte-identical, zero diff, no --update — plus new unit tests (test_preference.py) assert phase="pref" contributions never appear in the phase="base"/"cohort" filtered views.

S61 · Aug 3, 2026
The plan leaves no numeric minimum-data-density threshold for training (deliberately, per WP-14) — does that mean the pipeline has no guard against bad data at all?
No — a guard still exists, just not a product-density number. ghar_re_core/training/dataset.py's guard_sufficient_data() refuses to fit (raises, writes nothing) if there are zero real labeled rows, or if every labeled row shares the same class (logistic regression is structurally undefined with a single class — that's a correctness requirement, not a business judgement call). Separately, only data_source=="real" rows are ever used (ai_generated/stub rows are excluded categorically), and shown_not_tapped/edit/swap rows are excluded from labeling entirely rather than defaulted to a rejection label, per FD-11's no-fabricated-labels rule.

July 13, 2026
134 files moved · 6 created
The flat doc-garage/ dump (134 files recovered after the original repository was lost) was dissolved into a structured tree: docs/ split by document purpose, database/ split by SQL job, data/source/ for the original spreadsheets. What this does
Separates documents by what they are for: why the product exists (product), how it's built (architecture), rules that bind future work (governance), the data-research trail (research), plans (roadmaps), interactive explainers (visuals), and history — with proposals (work-packages) kept strictly apart from proof of execution (certificates).

→
Output

open file→ read header + status→ match against folder purpose table→ git mv (history kept)
Key line of code
Status: DESIGNED — awaiting Founder approval to execute ← this one line inside "REPO-WP-03D_Seed_Readiness_Certification" is why a file named "Certification" was filed as a work package, not a certificate
Why keep proposals and certificates in separate folders?
This project was burned before by "described" being mistaken for "verified." The folder boundary makes that mistake structurally hard: if it's in certificates/, it happened, with evidence; if it's in work-packages/, it's a plan.
Why do filenames still say "Copy of _ACTIVE__…"?
Renaming was out of scope — the instruction was to move files with history preserved, and DOC-P3-09 §06E forbids renaming documents without Founder direction. A future approved hygiene pass can clean the prefixes.

Why not fake the missing rollbacks to "complete" the folder?

New CLAUDE.md
▾
What this does
Every AI session in this repo now reads the same rulebook first: sync before working, place documents by content not filename, never delete superseded versions, and never mark a work package COMPLETED without a matching certificate.
Flow through it
session opens→ CLAUDE.md read first→ docs/README.md for orientation→ only task-relevant docs opened
Key line of code
A Work Package's Status may only read COMPLETED if a companion certificate exists ← the single rule that prevents "described" being mistaken for "done" — this project's most expensive historical failure mode
Why was this committed exactly as supplied instead of being improved?
The instruction demanded the Principal Engineer's exact content, no paraphrasing. The file was committed byte-for-byte as the Founder placed it.

What was built this session
July 13, 2026
WP-5C
The repository had rollback scripts for only 2 of its 28 migrations (027, 028) — the other 26 were either never written (001–020) or lost when the old repository was deleted (021–026). WP-5C authored all 26. Each rollback was rebuilt from its own forward migration file (the authoritative record of what that migration created) and reverses exactly that — nothing more. They are designed to run in reverse order (028→001) and use plain DROP so a mistake fails loudly instead of silently cascading, matching the existing 027/028 style. Five reversals carry loud warnings because undoing them on real data would lose or reject rows (the two slot array conversions, the tag-uniqueness restore, the extension drop, and the runtime-named partitions) — all safe on today's unseeded database. No forward migration, architecture, or live database was touched; the database was only read, never changed.

July 13, 2026
WP-5F
Every one of the 28 build scripts (migrations), 28 undo scripts (rollbacks), 3 sample-data files (seeds) and 6 self-test files (validation) was read from top to bottom — not skimmed, and not taken on trust from earlier sessions' reports. On paper, the blueprint is solid: the build scripts are numbered 001–028 with no gaps, each one only relies on tables an earlier script already made, and every single one has exactly one matching undo script (28 out of 28). Run in reverse, the undo scripts return the database to empty. Two real problems surfaced that earlier reports missed: (1) one sample-data file tries to load a meal-slot value the way the old schema stored it, but a later build script changed how that column works — so it would fail to load; (2) one self-test file still expects 60 tables when the recovered blueprint now has 62. Neither is an architecture flaw — both are leftovers from before the last six build scripts were added. Nothing was built, changed, or run against any database; this was a read-and-report pass only. Overall verdict: YELLOW — the core is sound, but the sample-data and self-test layers, plus some missing production scripts and execution proof, must be fixed before a green light.

WP-5D
The goal was to make the repository match production's engineering exactly. We read production's migration history (read-only — never touched or changed production) and found 3 scripts production has that the repo doesn't: (1) pf1 — a real security fix that closes the leftover-permission gap Session 7 measured; (2 & 3) two production data loads (real cuisines and ingredients) which are deliberately not kept in the repo (the repo uses small sample data instead). The security fix's exact text was recovered from production as evidence. But it can't be added to the repo yet: one of its lines locks down a hidden "auto-enable-security" helper that exists only in production, was never part of any tracked script, and actually conflicts with the repo's deliberate design (it switches on row-security for internal bookkeeping tables the design intentionally leaves off — production currently has security on 33 tables where the repo design expects 20). Adding it would either break the repo's from-scratch rebuild or silently change the frozen design — a call only the Founder should make. So this session recovered the evidence, classified everything, measured the gap (96.6% parity), and stopped short of guessing. No repository files changed.

WP-6RE · Read-only
The Founder asked for a forensic audit: prove, from repository evidence alone, whether the recommendation engine can be completely and deterministically seeded — and explicitly do not trust previous reports. This session finally read the five recommendation-engine design documents (RE-DOC-01–05), which had never been opened in any prior session, and re-derived every contested value from scratch.

The big result: the earlier conclusion — "the whole engine layer is blocked because key values are missing from the master workbook" — was too pessimistic and is now corrected. Most of those "missing" values are in fact derivable or recoverable, each with a traceable source: a meal-class's weekday/weekend type (from its fit scores, all 131 present), a persona's diet (from its nonveg mode plus a frozen business rule), the 2-letter state codes (already sitting in the regional-affinity file), the region grouping, and persona codes. Nothing in the engine's knowledge is truly absent.

Exactly one genuine blocker survives, and it's provable with simple arithmetic rather than opinion: the cohort table's own uniqueness rule (one row per persona + state + diet-mode) allows at most 1,476 rows, but the target is 2,952 — because the source splits every cohort into two city tiers that the table has no column to hold (this is the long-standing "GAP-002"). That is a real design decision for the Founder — add a city-tier column, or change the target — not a data problem. It blocks only the cohort table and the two big plan tables that depend on it (the 20,664-row weekly plan and the 7,992-row add-on plan). Everything else can be seeded. No database was touched and nothing was invented.

WP-6E · Data Gate
This was the proof-in-practice step. On a completely disposable local PostgreSQL database (never production — the production Supabase was deliberately not touched), the repository built the entire system from nothing: all 30 migrations applied cleanly, then the config, content and recommendation-engine seeds loaded. Crucially, the database's own triggers computed every derived value — each dish's diet type, jain status, allergen codes and food-DNA vector, plus the tag ordering — with no manual edits, and the results were spot-checked correct (chicken dish → non-veg; poha → vegan). The engine tables came out at their exact targets: 2,952 cohorts, 20,664 weekly-plan rows (exactly cohorts × 7), 7,992 household add-on rows.

Validation ran end to end: every foreign key resolved (zero orphans), the city-tier fix (GAP-002) held (2,952 unique cohorts, every one tagged with a tier), the safety checks found zero diet/allergen/jain violations, and the access rules correctly blocked anonymous writes and hid the engine's internal tables. Then the database was rolled all the way back to empty, and the whole thing was rebuilt identically on a second fresh database — proving it is deterministic and repeatable, not a one-off. During teardown, two small rollback gaps surfaced and were fixed with evidence (a missing undo for the config seed, and clearing an audit table before deleting dishes).

Verdict: DATA GATE PASSED for the Initial Canonical Dataset, certified as REPO-CERT-007. The project now officially exits Knowledge Engineering and is ready for Backend Engineering. Nothing was faked and nothing was hidden — two honest follow-ups remain (one table, the city-migration overlay, is deferred because a field is genuinely absent from the source; and a few self-tests are hardcoded to old illustrative data), both non-blocking.

WP-8A · DOC-P4-00
This was the first step of Phase 8 (Backend Engineering) — and deliberately architecture, not implementation. It produced a single comprehensive backend architecture document (DOC-P4-00), built strictly on top of the already-frozen design rather than inventing anything new. The backend is Supabase Edge Functions (Deno/TypeScript) over PostgreSQL, with two "surfaces": the mobile app reads safe tables directly (protected by row-level security), while everything touching the recommendation engine goes through custom functions exposing the 10 frozen API endpoints.

The document specifies a clean layered code structure (thin request handlers → business services → data repositories → database), the recommendation engine as an isolated, reusable module shared by both the live endpoint and the nightly plan-generation job, and one safety-critical rule made explicit: because these functions run with elevated privileges that bypass row-level security, every ownership check must be written into the code itself. It also covers authentication, validation, error handling, logging, configuration, transactions, caching, background jobs, testing, deployment (via the same numbered-migration discipline, with the safety gates as release blockers), versioning, rate limiting, observability, a future-AI path, and a scalability roadmap — all 30 requested topics.

It closes with a backend readiness score (8.5/10), risks (chiefly: don't miss an in-code authorization check, and the 800ms recommendation budget), a recommended build order, and a Phase-8 work-package roadmap (8B scaffolding → 8H hardening → the API Gate). No code, no endpoints, no schema or database changes — a blueprint for Founder approval before any implementation starts.

What was done this session
July 14, 2026
WP-6E.3 · REPO-CERT-010
The finding, root-caused (Phase 1). Last session flagged that on the new Supabase the app roles (anon/authenticated) could still write the dishes' derived, safety-critical columns (diet type, allergen flags, genome) — even though the certified security fix (migration 029) is recorded as applied. This session proved why, from evidence: the recorded migration genuinely did contain the REVOKEs, and the repo file was never edited. But Supabase's own platform default ("grant everything on new tables to the app roles") had put a full table-level grant on dishes at creation, and a table-level grant overrides column-level revokes — so on this freshly-provisioned project the certified lock-down simply wasn't in force. No later migration or data load re-granted anything. That is environment drift, not a repository defect. (Postgres doesn't journal grant changes, so the exact moment can't be timestamped — stated honestly, not guessed.)

The fix, done to scope (Phase 2). Only the missing privilege statements from migration 029 were applied — the exact repo-certified REVOKE/GRANT lines, nothing else (the production-only quarantined line stayed quarantined). Before/after was captured. After: anon/authenticated cannot write any dishes column and cannot run the derivation trigger functions; but they keep read access (the app still reads the catalog), the backend's full-access role is untouched, and row-level security is unchanged. No data, no counts, no schema touched.

The self-tests, modernized (Phase 3). The validation scripts still referenced the old removed sample rows ("Aloo Poha with Peanuts", "ADDON_INFANT"), a stale table-count, the pre-Option-C targets, and a wrong weekday spelling. Each was updated to the real canonical data — swapping in genuine dishes/classes that exercise the same logic, mapping the seed-gate targets to the approved ICD-1 scope, turning a brittle fixed count into a stronger "no table without security" check, and fixing the weekday format. Intent preserved, accuracy improved, nothing weakened — two checks actually became stricter.

Regression (Phase 4). The full suite (900–905) was re-run on the live database and passes end to end: 62 tables, all 15 seed gates exact, all foreign keys clean (zero orphans), derivations correct, the propagate trigger proven on real data, the app roles now correctly blocked from writing derived columns, RLS intact, GAP-002 satisfied, and the end-to-end smoke test resolving a real weekly plan. The only two "skips" are tests that need seeded login fixtures (which don't exist until the auth flow is built) — exactly as in the original certification. The one test that temporarily edits an ingredient reverted cleanly; every count and derivation is unchanged.

What this does

Key line of code
Verdict: B — Mostly Implemented with Minor Gaps ← the headline finding was actually reassuring: the team's own "stop rather than guess" discipline (WP-8D→8E→8F→8FA) was found to be working exactly as designed
Why does the audit trust a "B" grade rather than treat every gap as a failure?
Because almost every gap it found (unratified documents, the stale README, the one open CandidateRepository decision) was something the repository's own paper trail had already disclosed before the audit began — a team whose own records catch its own gaps doesn't need an auditor to discover them for the first time, it needs the discipline to close them.
Why audit a branch that had diverged from origin/main?
The Founder explicitly selected that branch (`feat/wp-8f-runtime-blocker`) as the authoritative base for this audit, since it carried the WP-8F/8FA work origin/main didn't yet have — the divergence is disclosed in the report's own §0 rather than silently audited around.

DB database/migrations/031_dish_ingredients_main_ingredient_flag.sql, 032_interaction_events_dedup_key.sql
▾
What this does
031 adds a plain boolean column so any dish-ingredient row can be flagged as a "main" ingredient (a dish can have more than one). 032 adds a client-supplied dedup key plus a partitioned unique index so a retried event submission is recognized instead of counted twice.
Input → Output
Input
Founder-approved SER-002/SER-003 change requests.
→
Output
Two live schema changes, each re-verified against the real database afterward.
Flow through it
SER-002/SER-003 approved→ mcp__supabase__apply_migration→ live column/index confirmed via information_schema/pg_inherits
Key line of code
ALTER TABLE public.dish_ingredients ADD COLUMN is_main_ingredient boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false; ← every one of the 7,108 existing rows became false automatically — nothing was guessed or backfilled by this migration alone
Why a plain boolean instead of a rank or weight column?
The rule for deciding which ingredient "dominates" a dish (by weight, by listing order, or a curated list) was still unratified at migration time — a rank/weight column would have presupposed one specific rule. A boolean is the minimum structure that works under any of them, including multiple true rows per dish.
Why can't the dedup key fully guarantee no double-counted event?
The events table is partitioned by month, and Postgres requires the partition key inside any unique index on a partitioned table — so the DB-level guarantee only holds within one partition. The Founder approved a two-layer design: this index for the common case, plus a 24-hour app-level lookback check (not yet built) for the rare cross-partition case.

Why not design a dedicated swipe-weighting formula?

New supabase/functions/_shared/services/adapters/supabase-stores.ts — SupabaseCandidateRepository
▾
What this does
Implements both methods of the CandidateRepository port (getClassCandidates, getPopularFallback), fetching real dish rows and joining ingredients/tags/cuisine to fill every field the engine's scoring code expects — with flat queries and in-memory joins, since no foreign keys exist to support Supabase's relational-embedding shortcut.
Input → Output
Input
A meal-class ID, plus the dishes/dish_ingredients/dish_tags/cuisines tables.
→
Output
A list of DishCandidate objects, each with all 17 fields the engine's scoring code needs.
Flow through it
loadDishes / loadAllergenMarks / loadTags / loadCuisineGroups→ assemble() joins them in memory→ 17-field DishCandidate returned
Key line of code
const MAIN_INGREDIENT_CLASS_PRIORITY = [...] ← applies DOC-P3-13's documented priority order verbatim when a dish has more than one main-ingredient tag, rather than picking one arbitrarily
Why not use Supabase's relational-embedding query syntax (e.g. .select("ingredients(name)"))?
Verified via pg_constraint that no foreign key exists on dish_ingredients.ingredient_id, dish_tags.tag_id, or re_class_dish_options.dish_id — embedding syntax would silently fail to resolve. Flat queries plus in-memory joins were used instead, and this reasoning is recorded directly in the adapter's own code comment.
What happens to fields with no real source at all?
seasonalAffinity always returns empty (WP-8FA already found no source exists anywhere) and hasNonHalalMeat uses a documented fail-closed proxy (hasPork OR mainIngredientClass='meat') — both explicitly labeled as deferrals/proxies in the code and this certificate, never silently presented as real data.

DBghar_re schema — migrations 034–037
▾
What this does
Creates a brand-new, isolated database schema for the rebuilt engine: dishes and their ingredients/tags, households and their derived profile, safety tables, and the editable knowledge base the engine reads. It does not touch the old retired engine's tables.
Input → Output

The frozen Ghar RE v1.0 design — no live tables to migrate, a clean-slate build.
→

A new, isolated ghar_re schema (28 tables) the engine can read from, fully separate from the old retired tables.

data_source ghar_re.data_source_kind NOT NULL ← every table must say whether each row is real, AI-generated, or a stub — no silent defaults
Why a separate schema instead of reusing the existing tables?
The old persona/cohort engine is fully retired; a clean isolated schema means the rebuild can't accidentally depend on or corrupt the old data, and can be reviewed like new code.
Newghar_re_core — the engine (Python)
▾
What this does
The single tested implementation of the recommendation maths: it turns a household's raw Q1–Q15 answers into a profile, removes dishes the household can't eat, scores the rest against taste/region/weather, pairs them, and returns exactly 7 ranked meal plates. 16 tests cover it.
Input → Output
Input
A household's raw Q1–Q15 answers plus the dish catalogue and context (weather, day).
→
Output
Exactly 7 ranked meal plates, each with a score and its contributing factors.
Flow through it
answers→profile (D1–D7)→filter→score→pair→7 plates
Key line of code
plates = pairing.assemble_7(cat, theta, ctx, objective, n=7) ← builds the 7 ranked plates for one household
Why is this a separate installable package?
So the maths live in exactly one place. The web service and any future tool import this package rather than re-implementing formulas, which is what prevents two slightly different engines drifting apart.
Newghar_re_service — HTTP host + contract
▾
What this does
A thin FastAPI service that hosts the engine over HTTP. At startup it loads the dish catalogue and config through swappable "providers", then serves POST /v1/recommendations plus health/readiness checks. A JSON-Schema contract pins the exact request/response shape, with an open "contributions" list so new score factors don't break callers.
Input → Output
Input
A contract-validated JSON request from the edge function (household answers + context).
→
Output
A contract-validated JSON response carrying the engine's 7 ranked plates.
Flow through it
startup: load config + catalogue→validate request→call engine→validate + return response
Key line of code
POST /v1/recommendations → engine.run(payload, catalogue, config, registry) ← the route just translates; the engine does the work
Why a locked contract file both sides validate against?
The app and the engine are written in different languages; a shared schema they each check against is what stops them quietly disagreeing on the request/response shape over time.
Newrecommendations edge function (orchestration)
▾
What this does
The Supabase edge function that sits between the app and the engine. It authenticates the caller, builds the household's answers into a request, validates it, calls the engine with a signed security header, and passes the 7 plates back to the app. If the engine times out or fails, it returns a safe fallback meal as a normal success instead of an error.
Input → Output
Input
An authenticated app request for today's meal ideas.
→
Output
7 ranked meal plates on success, or one safe fallback plate (never an error) if the engine is unreachable.
Flow through it
authenticate→compose + validate→signed call (2.5s, retry once)→pass through / fallback
Key line of code
x-ghar-signature: t=<time>,v1=<hmac-sha256(secret, "<time>.<body>")> ← the signature that proves the request really came from the app's server
Why return a fallback plate instead of an error when the engine is down?
A hungry user should still see familiar food, not a broken screen. The failure is logged, but the user experience degrades gracefully.
Next session
Live household/event tables location decision, engine-side signature verification, then observability (Phase D) and deployment (Phase F).

If a recommendation call went wrong, there was no reliable way to find every log line for that ONE request — the edge function's own id and the "request id" used in business logs could silently differ, the recommendation engine logged almost nothing about a request's timing, and a household that legitimately couldn't reach 7 meal plates was invisible — not tracked as its own outcome anywhere.
→
✅ After this session
One request id now appears on every log line on both sides, from the moment a call arrives to the moment it responds. Every log line says how long the recommendation-engine call took and how it ended (success / partial / timeout / fallback / error). Simple built-in counters exist on both sides — no new monitoring service — and a household that gets fewer than 7 plates now shows up as its own tracked "partial" outcome, not lumped in with real errors.

Phase D · observability only
This is Phase D from the frozen RE-DOC-10 phase table — observability only, explicitly not deployment or CI/CD (those are Phase F, later). Four things:

1. One id, everywhere. The edge function's business-level "request id" and its infrastructure-level "trace id" could previously diverge if a caller sent a custom one. Fixed by (a) binding the request id onto a "child logger" the moment it's known, so every subsequent log line inherits it automatically instead of each call site having to remember to add it, and (b) teaching the very first line of the edge function to also recognise the industry-standard X-Request-Id header (it only looked for x-trace-id before), so the id is consistent from the first log line, not just from the business logic onward. Verified live: a test call with X-Request-Id: demo-req-42 produced 6 log lines across the whole request — auth, compose, RE-call, response — every one carrying demo-req-42.

2. Every log line now says how it ended and how long it took. The recommendation engine (Python) previously logged almost nothing about a request — no "request received" line, no timing, and a crash inside it wasn't even caught or logged. Now every path (received → validated/rejected → computed/crashed → responded) is logged with a `service` name, an `outcome`, and how many milliseconds it took. On the edge function side, the call to the recommendation engine previously wasn't timed at all on success — only a timeout produced a log line. Now the actual wait time is measured on the edge function's own clock (the real user-facing one) and attached to every outcome, success included.

3. Simple built-in counters, nothing fancy. Both sides now count requests/successes/partial-results/errors/fallbacks in memory — no metrics database, no dashboard. The recommendation engine exposes its counters on its existing /v1/meta endpoint (checked live: after one test call it correctly reported requests_total: 1, success_total: 1). The edge function logs a periodic one-line summary every 50 requests instead, since it doesn't have an equivalent endpoint to extend. Both are deliberately throwaway — meant to be replaced once Phase F picks real monitoring, not a design commitment.

4. "Not quite enough plates" is now its own category. If a household can only be served fewer than 7 meal plates, the recommendation engine already noted this in a `warnings` list, but the edge function's own logging treated it exactly the same as a full success, and there was no separate counter for it. Now both sides recognise this as a distinct "partial" outcome — logged and counted separately from both hard errors and from full 7-plate successes.

July 28, 2026
Phase C.5 · prerequisite for Phase F
This session ran the work originally scoped as "Phase C.5", which had been skipped when Phases D and E ran ahead of it. The deployment-topology audit confirmed both of its gaps were still open, and both had to close before any deployment work — not after.

1. The engine now checks who is calling it. The app was already signing every request to the recommendation engine with a shared secret (like a tamper-proof wax seal). The engine, however, never opened the seal — it just trusted whatever arrived. That made the whole security model one-sided: the plan assumed the engine would only ever be reachable from the app, but nothing enforced either half. The engine now verifies the seal on every recommendation request and rejects four distinct cases: no signature at all, a malformed one, a valid signature over different content (i.e. someone modified the request in transit), and a correctly-signed request that is more than 5 minutes old (someone replaying a captured request). Crucially, the rejection happens before the request is even read or any calculation is done. Health-check endpoints stay open on purpose — the hosting platform needs to ping those before any secret exists, and requiring a signature there is how a deployment locks itself out. Proven working across both languages: a signature generated by the real app code was fed to the engine and accepted, and the same signature with one extra byte added to the content was correctly rejected.

2. Real household data, not a hardcoded sample. Every recommendation was previously built from the same fake household. The honest finding here was that the live database already had most of what was needed under different names — so rather than create six new tables as originally sketched, this session verified what already existed and added only the four that genuinely didn't. The user's profile already is the household (it holds home state, city, diet, religious preference and allergies), and the household-members table already existed. Creating a second "households" table would have split household identity in two. What was actually missing: the remaining onboarding answers, the per-request context, a table to record what was recommended, and a table to record user feedback. A brand-new user with no profile yet is treated as a valid case, not an error — they get neutral defaults and a real recommendation instead of an error screen. One honest note carried into the code: member ages aren't collected by the current onboarding flow, so the engine gets a role-based stand-in age; this is safe because the safety-critical rules (baby food, elderly spice limits) key off the member's role, which is real data.

3. Automatic Python code checking. Phase E had left an explicit placeholder noting no Python linter had been chosen. This session added two standard tools (ruff for bugs/style, mypy for type errors) and wired them into the automated checks. The first real run flagged 223 issues. Rather than blanket-silencing them, each was triaged: everything in the service layer was properly fixed, and for the frozen recommendation math — whose exact output is deliberately locked by the golden-master test — only the rules that catch real bugs were kept on, with cosmetic ones switched off and the reason documented in the config. Two genuine dead-code findings in the math were fixed safely; the golden-master test then confirmed the recommendations were byte-for-byte unchanged, which is exactly the proof that matters.

One real latent bug found and deliberately NOT fixed. The linter surfaced a genuine gap in the plate-pairing rules: the "protein balance" bonus declares four qualifying food categories (dal, kebab, egg dish, curry) but the code only ever checks one of them (dal). So a curry- or kebab-based plate silently misses a bonus it was designed to get. Fixing it is a one-line change — but it would change what food gets recommended, which is a food-quality decision for the Founder, not something to slip into a code-cleanup task. It has been left in place with a clear explanatory note in the code, and the golden-master test will fail loudly the moment anyone changes it, forcing the change into review. That is the golden master doing precisely the job it was built for.
