July 29, 2026
Phase F · prepared, NOT deployed
1. A sealed, versioned data bundle. The engine needs three things that don't live inside its own code: seven settings files, an ingredient master list (which drives allergy and Jain safety checks), and the data contract it shares with the app. All three were being found by "look in the folder next to me" — which works in a code checkout and fails the moment the engine is packaged up and moved. A new export step now snapshots all of it into one bundle with a version stamp. That stamp is a fingerprint of the contents, not a timestamp: the same data always produces the same stamp, so comparing two servers is a one-line check rather than guesswork. The stamp shows up on the engine's status endpoint and in its startup logs.

2. A container recipe with everything pinned. Written as a two-stage build so the tools used to assemble it don't ship inside the final result. Every version is nailed down exactly — Python and all four dependencies — because a rebuild that silently picks up a newer library is how a working system quietly stops working. It runs as a non-root user and writes nothing to disk. The build itself fails if the data bundle didn't make it in, rather than producing an image that only breaks once it's live and serving people.

3. Server configuration for Fly.io. Configured to always keep at least one machine running — deliberately not the cheaper "shut down when idle" mode, because this sits in the path of every single recommendation and a cold start would be a delay the user feels. Two separate health checks: one asking "is the process alive?" and a different one asking "has it finished loading its data?". Using the wrong one for the wrong job is a classic way to create a server that restarts forever without ever finishing startup. No public address is configured, so it isn't reachable from the open internet.

4. Secrets kept out of the repository. The shared secret the app and engine use to prove calls are genuine is set through Fly's encrypted secret store, never committed. Exact commands are in the runbook, including a way to keep the value out of your shell history. This is the only secret the engine needs — it holds no database credentials at all, by design.

A real bug this session caught — and the reason it was caught. Rather than just writing the container recipe and declaring it done, the engine was installed and run under the container's actual conditions, with the project folder unreachable. It crashed — on a third file nobody had noticed: the ingredient master list, read at startup through its own hardcoded path. Reviewing the code alone had found two such paths; running it found the third. That file is now part of the bundle and the engine starts cleanly.

S39 · Ghar RE Phase F follow-up — the engine opens to the internet, guarded by its signature check
Settled how the app actually reaches the engine: it will be publicly reachable, and the signed-request check is now the only thing protecting it — so that check was itself given a shield against being flooded.
⛔ Before this session
The server configuration was written assuming the engine would sit on a private network that only our own app could reach, with the signed-request check as a backup layer behind it. But that plan could not actually work: the part of our app that calls the engine runs on Supabase's servers, which cannot join a private network on Fly and cannot even promise a fixed set of addresses to allow through. So the deployment was blocked on an unanswered question, and the instructions told you to expect no public address.
→
✅ After this session
The question is answered and written down as a decision: the engine is reachable over the public internet, encrypted, and the signed-request check is the real and only gate. Because that check is now the only thing in the way, it no longer stands alone in the open — a limiter in front of it caps how many requests any single source can make per minute, so a flood is turned away cheaply instead of making the engine do expensive signature maths thousands of times. The deployment instructions now match what will actually happen, including the fact that a public address showing up is correct rather than a mistake.

July 29, 2026
Phase F follow-up · still NOT deployed
1. The networking decision, recorded as a decision. Last session left one genuinely open question: could the app actually reach the engine on a private network? The answer is no — Supabase's servers can't join Fly's private network, and they can't guarantee a fixed list of addresses we could allow through instead. So the engine accepts public traffic. What matters is that this is now written down as a settled choice with its reasoning, not left as a gap someone later has to rediscover. The configuration file and the runbook were both corrected to say the same thing.

2. Traffic is now encrypted in transit. Previously the setting that forces encrypted connections was deliberately switched off, on the reasoning that a private network already encrypts everything. That reasoning no longer holds, so it was switched on. This matters more than it sounds: the requests carry household composition — who lives there, ages, dietary and allergy information — which is personal data and has no business crossing the internet readable.

3. A limiter in front of the signature check. With the signature check now the only gate, anything on the internet can make the engine do cryptographic work simply by sending it something. The limiter caps each source to 300 requests a minute and turns away the excess before any of that work happens. The ordering is the entire point — placed the other way round it would be decoration, since the expensive step would already have run. That ordering is deliberately locked in by a test, because it depends on a subtle framework behaviour that a future well-meaning tidy-up could easily reverse without noticing.

4. Four judgement calls inside the limiter worth knowing about. The cap is deliberately generous, because our app's traffic arrives from a small number of shared addresses — many real users can look like one caller, so a tight cap would throttle customers rather than attackers; it's adjustable without rebuilding anything. Health checks are exempt, because turning away the platform's "are you alive?" probe would get the machine killed and restarted — a protection causing the exact outage it exists to prevent. If the limiter fails to load, traffic passes through, whereas if the security secret is missing the engine refuses to start; a missing safety damper shouldn't cause an outage, but a missing lock must never be treated as an open door. And its memory is capped, because remembering one entry per address is itself a way to exhaust the machine when the addresses are attacker-chosen.

A contradiction found in last session's configuration. The previous file carried a comment stating there was intentionally no public entry point — while the block that creates a public entry point sat twenty lines below it. On Fly, that block is precisely the public service declaration. So the private-only intention was never actually achieved by the file; a deploy would have been publicly reachable regardless of what the comment claimed. Harmless now that public access is the deliberate choice, but the wrong comment was recorded and corrected rather than quietly deleted, because anyone who had read it was misled about what would ship.

S41 · Security hotfix — closing the household-ownership gap the audit found
The gap the last session found and deliberately did not fix — any signed-in user could ask for another household's recommendation data by supplying its id — is closed. One import, one function call, placed before any data is fetched.
⛔ Before this session
A signed-in user could send a request for someone else's household by putting that household's id straight in the request body, and the recommendations endpoint would fetch and serve that other household's data without checking whether the caller actually owned it. The check needed to stop this already existed elsewhere in this exact codebase — it is what protects the consent endpoint — but nobody had wired it into this one. A leftover code comment blamed a missing database table for the gap, but that table had existed for two sessions; the real reason was simply that the call was never made.
→
✅ After this session
The exact same ownership check the consent endpoint already uses now runs on every recommendation request, before any household or context data is fetched — a caller asking for a household that isn't theirs is refused immediately, and nothing downstream (the data fetch, the engine call, the event log) ever runs. The stale comment is gone. Three new tests prove it: a mismatched id is refused and nothing downstream fires, a caller's own id is allowed through normally, and leaving the id off (the common case) still defaults to the caller's own household exactly as before.

Security hotfix — smallest possible change, nothing else touched
1. The ownership check, wired in. The exact same function the consent endpoint already calls — already tested, already proven correct — is now called on the recommendations endpoint too, with the same pattern: same import, same call, same error on failure. It runs immediately after figuring out which household the request is asking about, and before anything is fetched from the database.

2. Placement matters here. The check runs before the household/context data is loaded, before the request is sent to the recommendation engine, and before anything is written to the event history. An unauthorized request now stops at the very first gate — it never touches a database read, an engine call, or a log write for data it had no right to see.

3. The stale comment is gone. The old comment said the fix was blocked on a database table that "doesn't exist yet." That table has existed since the tables were built two sessions ago — the real blocker was only that nobody had made the call. Left uncorrected, a future session could have trusted that comment over the actual code and assumed there was nothing to fix.

4. Three tests, one for each outcome that matters. A request for a household the caller does not own is refused, and none of the downstream work happens (proven by counting calls to the data-fetch, the engine call, and the event write — all three stay at zero). A request for the caller's own household still works normally. And the common case — no household id supplied at all, which defaults to the caller's own — still works exactly as it did before this change.

1. A new endpoint, built the same way the last two were. Same wiring pattern as the consent and recommendations endpoints — nothing new invented, just the same shape applied a third time. It accepts however many answers a caller has ready, logs each one to a permanent history, and keeps a running "current state" view that updates incrementally rather than requiring everything at once.

2. Same ownership rule as the security fix, applied from day one. A caller can only ever write their own household's data — checked before a single write happens, the same import and the same pattern the security fix just proved out. For the very first creation of a household specifically, there's a second, even stronger guarantee underneath that check: the actual database command that creates the record is hard-wired to use the logged-in person's own identity, not anything read from the request — so even a bug in the check above couldn't let it create a record for the wrong person.

3. Nothing invented, ever, if the answer isn't known yet. The household record can't be created until five specific pieces of information are all known — and if one is still missing, the endpoint simply doesn't create it yet rather than filling the gap with a guess. This was the standing rule already established elsewhere in this project (never fabricate a value a real user hasn't actually provided), applied here for the first time to a brand-new write path rather than an existing one.

4. A genuinely resumable flow, not a one-shot form. Answers given today and answers given next week both count — a table already built two sessions ago for exactly this purpose (an append-only log of every answer, one row per question) turned out to be the right place to accumulate partial progress, so nothing new had to be invented for it. Family member details (children, elders, their specific needs) can only be added once the household itself exists, since one literally depends on the other existing first — attempting it out of order is refused with a clear, specific error rather than a confusing failure.

Why is this order different from the official design document?
The design document asks about household members before the basic profile is complete. The backend rejects that — it hard-requires the profile to exist first. Rather than silently working around it or building a screen guaranteed to fail on first use, the order was changed here and flagged as an open question for whoever owns the design document.
Why free-text boxes for some questions instead of nice pick-lists?
A few questions (non-veg types eaten, veg days, health conditions) don't have a fixed official list of choices anywhere in the codebase yet. Rather than inventing one that might not match what the backend actually expects, this session used plain text boxes and flagged it — a real pick-list can be added once that official list exists.

July 30, 2026
Feature branch: claude/phase-g-catalogue-migration-kppmgx — NOT on main, review pending
1. The real menu, transformed into the shape the engine already expects. A new script reads the actual 810-dish spreadsheet the catalogue team authored and turns every row into exactly the same data shape the old 39-dish sample used — so nothing about how the engine scores or pairs dishes had to change, only where the dishes come from. Fields the spreadsheet genuinely doesn't have (which meals are "dry," "liquid," or a full standalone meal; whether a dish is vegetarian; whether it's Jain-safe) are worked out from what the spreadsheet does have, with the exact reasoning written down in the code, not hidden. Fields nobody has an honest way to know yet (detailed nutrition breakdowns, a few Jain/allergen edge cases) are left blank rather than guessed at.

2. The deployable image now bakes in the real menu, not the sample. The same build step that packages the engine for deployment was pointed at the new real-menu script instead of the 39-dish sample, and actually re-run — an earlier pass in this same branch had only proven the code path worked without checking the packaged file itself still had the old 39-dish sample sitting in it. Caught and fixed in the same branch: the real, 810-dish version is what's actually committed now.

3. Two bugs the real menu exposed, found with evidence and fixed, not guessed at. First: the engine crashed on any real dish with no iconicity score, because it had no concept of "not scored yet" — only "scored." Fixed so an unscored dish is simply treated as contributing nothing extra, which is what the underlying scoring formula already intends for a missing term. Second, more serious: two out of every three real dishes were silently being treated as "region unknown," because the lookup table that says "this cuisine belongs to this region" only ever knew about the 10 cuisines in the old sample, not the 57 real ones. Proven concretely: one household — a vegetarian Jain couple — could only ever get 3 of the 7 meal suggestions the engine is supposed to produce, because "region unknown" was quietly blocking most valid pairings. Fixed by teaching the engine every real cuisine's actual region; that same household now gets all 7, and the fix was checked to prove nothing else about the existing, already-correct 39-dish sample was disturbed by it.

4. sig_scores_v1.csv — a file the engine's own documentation has always assumed exists — finally does. The engine's knowledge base has referenced this file by name from the day it was written, as the source of how iconic or ordinary each of the 810 dishes is (a "world-famous" Butter Chicken should be recommended differently than a "plain steamed rice"). It never actually existed anywhere in the repository until this work. A companion effort built it — an automatic best-guess score for most dishes, based on how well-known their cuisine is, and a shortlist of 63 dishes (including Butter Chicken and Dal Makhani themselves) flagged for a human to actually confirm, since "is this dish famous across all of India" isn't something any spreadsheet column can answer by itself. This session brought that file over and taught the real-menu script to actually read it, instead of the rough 12-dish guess it was using before.

5. Proven, not just claimed, that nothing here breaks the existing rules. The frozen API contract — the exact shape every response is allowed to take — was re-checked against real responses built from the real 810-dish menu, across all 7 sample households and multiple contexts, and it holds with zero violations. A second check confirmed the service's own scoring math still matches the engine's core math exactly, dish for dish, across 516 real dishes — no silent drift between the two.

Modified supabase/functions/_shared/api/handler.ts
▾
What this does
This is the one shared wrapper every Edge Function is built from. It now recognizes a browser's CORS preflight request (an OPTIONS request browsers automatically send before certain real requests) and answers it directly with the right permissions — instead of letting it fall through to the login check, which was always going to reject it since preflight requests never carry a login token.
Input → Output
Input
A live log showing a real browser signup getting "OPTIONS | 401" repeatedly right after login
→
Output
Preflight now answered before the login check runs; redeployed live to all 3 client-facing functions
Flow through it
real signup logs showed OPTIONS/401→ traced to defineHandler's missing CORS handling→ fixed in the one shared file→ redeployed to household/recommendations/consent
Key line of code
if (req.method === "OPTIONS") return new Response(null, { status: 204, headers: corsHeaders(req) }); ← answered before any login/auth code runs
Why didn't this show up before now?
Only a browser (web) client triggers a CORS preflight at all — the native mobile app's network layer never does. Nobody had tested the web target with a real login until this session.
New supabase/functions/_shared/auth/service-role.ts
▾
What this does
Checks that a request to one of the two scheduled data-deletion functions carries the project's own private service credential — not a regular user's login token, not nothing at all. Without this, the functions were completely open the moment they were deployed.
Input → Output
Input
2 functions with no auth check and a gateway setting that disabled even basic login verification
→
Output

Flow through it

Key line of code
if (!timingSafeEqual(token, ctx.config.supabaseServiceRoleKey)) throw ... ← rejects anything except the exact project credential, compared in a way that can't leak timing information
Why not just re-enable the standard login check instead of building something new?
The standard login check only verifies a regular user's token — it has no way to verify the special service credential these jobs are meant to use, and would actually reject it. A dedicated check was the only way to actually restrict this to the scheduler.

S48 · Compositional cohort plan + full dish→class coverage (WP-17)
The recommendation engine now works out a family's meal plan the way a nutritionist would — starting from who they are (e.g. "a Maharashtra family with a toddler"), grounding it in their region's real food, and then keeping it mild and child-friendly — instead of just averaging what's popular everywhere.
⛔ Before this session
The engine leaned on a "what's most common" model that washed out what makes a household's plan its own, so a Maharashtra toddler family's suggestions looked like the generic national average. And only 1 in 4 dishes was even linked to a meal type, so most dishes were invisible to the plan.
→
✅ After this session
The engine identifies the household's persona, builds their plan from that persona's preferred meal types, grounds it in their home state's real dishes (Pitla-Bhakri, Coconut-Stew for Maharashtra), and softens it for toddlers/elders. Every one of the 810 dishes is now correctly categorised, so the whole catalogue can participate.

1. Nutritionist/chef dish classifier (#5). A new offline step reads each meal class's authored example dishes and profile (slot, diet, heaviness, region) and scores every one of the 810 catalogue dishes against every compatible class — anchored on the dish's hero ingredient (a "Fish Curry" is classed by the fish, never as a chicken dish). Coverage went from 202/810 to 810/810, each row tagged as authored-truth or derived, with a confidence score.

2. Compositional cohort plan (WP-17 core). A new layer resolves the household's persona live (e.g. P10 "family with toddler"), takes that persona's preferred meal classes as the plan core, grounds them in the home state's regional dishes, adds a migration overlay for people living away from home, then reshapes for lifecycle (mild/child-friendly for toddlers, lighter for elders) and diet. The old "most popular" model is now a secondary smoother (70% new plan / 30% old model).

3. Proof it works. A Maharashtra/Pune family with a toddler now self-arrives at the exact target persona and a plan led by child-mild and traditional-Maharashtrian classes — the S14_T1_P10 shape the founder wanted, derived from the masters, not copied. 43 core + 62 service tests pass; per-user decision logs regenerated.

12 things touched

1. Multi-membership dish→class fix (WP-17.1 — the headline). The recommendation engine plans in 131 behavioural meal classes, but each catalogue dish was mapped to exactly one class — a strict partition. That structurally starved the behavioural dinner (DN_) classes: 24 of 131 classes (including 9 dinner classes such as child-friendly dinner) had zero dishes, so a plan that picked one of them had nothing to reconcile to and fell back to regional lunch/dinner plates. Now the offline classifier emits secondary memberships too, so a dish carries one primary class plus any secondary classes it also genuinely fits (top matches above a confidence floor, capped at 4 per dish, diet- and slot-gated). Result: the dish→class map went from 810 to 1485 membership rows (708 secondary), empty classes fell from 24 to 6, and child-friendly dinner went from 1 dish to 5. All 116 tests pass.

2. Why only 6 classes stay empty. The remaining 6 are legitimately empty and are meant to be — one is a combo-template class (compound plates, not single dishes) and the rest are gated/thin-catalogue classes (fasting, infant, northeast, oats). Force-filling them would pollute the plan, and the engine already skips any zero-dish class.

3. WP-18 backend planning surfaces (the user's concurrent work in the same commit). A new translation-only planning layer (meal_planner.py) and five signed RE endpoints now expose the full onboarding→plan→recipe flow: cold-start (15 diverse top dishes to seed likes), a slot's eligible options, a 7-day class plan (top dish-backed classes per slot), class-dishes reconciliation (only dishes whose class-set contains the chosen class — the multi-membership fix is what makes this return real dishes), and a full recipe with a Cloudinary image. Dish images are built deterministically from the dish name and are env-configurable; recipes are baked offline from each dish's real ingredients and times, quantities kept "to taste" with no gram amounts invented.

The engine had a synonyms table but no sourced, regionalised alias data in it, so cross-region users saw names they didn't know for dishes they eat every week.
→

4 things touched · commit aa841f5

1. Dish-name alias ontology (WP-19 — the headline). The catalogue's canonical dish names are often the regionally-marked form that users from other states don't recognise (Bharli Vangi = Bharwa Baingan in Hindi = Gutti Vankaya in Telugu = Ennegayi in Kannada). Migration 045 extends the existing ghar_re.dish_name_synonyms table into a sourced, regionalised alias ontology — adding alias_type, region, language, source_url and confidence, plus an index on region and a check constraint requiring every web-researched ('real') alias to carry a source_url. The constraint is added NOT VALID so a legacy uncited row can't make the migration fail on first apply, while still enforcing the citation rule on every new or updated row.

2. First cited, web-researched batch (seed 122). 37 web-researched aliases across 8 dishes — Bharli Vangi, Poha, Baingan Bharta, Pithla, Chole, Puran Poli, Dhokla and Undhiyu. Every row carries its alias_type/region/language/source_url/confidence, is tagged data_source='real', and inserts idempotently via ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. A safety filter drops any candidate alias that is itself a DISTINCT catalogue dish (Obbattu/Bobbatlu) so the ontology never conflates two genuinely different dishes. Validation 907 fail-loud checks that the WP-19 columns exist, every WP-19 'real' alias has a source_url and confidence, alias_type is a valid kind, and there are no orphan aliases.

3. Tested end-to-end, not yet deployed. Full cycle exercised on a throwaway Postgres 16: first apply (even with a legacy uncited 'real' row present), seed, validation PASS, three negative constraint tests correctly REJECTED (uncited real / bad alias_type / confidence out of range), rollback, and clean re-apply. The app suite stays 116/116 green (WP-19 is SQL-only). Recorded honestly: the migration is built and fully tested locally and deploy-ready, but was NOT applied to production — this environment has no Supabase CLI/MCP/credentials and the repo requires Founder-approved production deploys.

4. What's still pending. Only 8 of 810 dishes have researched aliases so far — the rest of the catalogue is to be filled by continued cited-research batches. Richer aliases also feed classify_dishes.py, which reads a dish's synonyms, so better alias coverage should improve dish→class matching down the line.

▾
What this does
The conductor. It runs each check in order, saves the raw evidence for each into a dated report folder, then adds up the results into a single score and a launch verdict. It is deliberately honest: a check it cannot run here is recorded as "skipped" or "blocked" with the reason, never counted as a pass.
Input → Output
Input
The repository, plus optional settings for a database URL or web address.
→
Output
A timestamped report folder (summary.txt/md/html + JSON) and a pass/fail exit code.
Flow through it
inventory→run each suite→collect evidence→score + verdict
Key line of code
can_launch = not hard_blockers and not unverified ← the app is only "launchable" if nothing failed AND no critical surface is unverified.
Why block launch on unverified surfaces, not just failures?
For a system meant to serve millions, "we never checked the delete/export path or the database" is a launch risk, not a pass. Saying "not certifiable here" is the honest answer.
Newpersonas/personas.py
▾
What this does
Defines 15 test households: the 7 shipped sample households plus 8 tricky ones — a strict Jain, a peanut-allergic person, a fasting household, a diabetic senior, a family with an infant, and deliberately broken inputs. Each carries what the app must do for it (e.g. "never serve non-veg", "must return a clean error").
Input → Output
Input
The real recommendation request contract.
→
Output
A list of personas the behaviour tests iterate over.
Flow through it
golden households+edge/malformed→expectations
Key line of code
forbid_diet=("non_veg",) ← a vegetarian/Jain household must never be served a non-veg dish.
Why include deliberately broken households?
To prove bad input produces a clean error (422), never a server crash (500) — the difference between a graceful app and one that falls over in front of a user.
Modifiedsuites/test_recommendation_behavior.py
▾
What this does
Sends each persona to the live recommendation service and checks the answer as a black box: no non-veg for veg households, no allergens, exactly 7 distinct plates in ranked order, and the same request twice gives the same answer. It never inspects the scoring maths.
Input → Output
Input
A persona household + context.
→
Output
Pass/fail on each behavioural rule.
Flow through it
sign request→POST /v1/recommendations→resolve dishes→assert rules
Key line of code
assert not violations, f"{persona.key}: served forbidden diet(s)" ← fails loudly if a forbidden dish reaches the plate.
Why black-box and not test the formula?
The brief requires it, and it is the right call: behaviour is what users experience. A formula can change; "a Jain is never served non-veg" must never change.
Newrunner/report_reader.py
▾
What this does
Reads the latest report and lists every failure worst-first, so a human knows exactly what to fix. It can also re-run only the checks that failed, so a fix is re-validated in seconds instead of re-running everything.
Input → Output
Input
A report folder's results file.
→
Output
A ranked triage list; optionally a re-run of only the failing suites.
Flow through it
load results→rank by severity→rerun failed (optional)
Key line of code
ranked.sort(key=lambda t: t[0]) ← puts the most severe (P0) failures at the top of the triage list.
Why not auto-edit the code to fix failures?
A quality tool that silently rewrites the code it is testing can't be trusted. It surfaces exactly what to fix and re-verifies after a human/agent fixes it.
Next session
Run the gate in CI with a live database and Deno, and against a running mobile web build, to certify the surfaces that are only "skipped/blocked" today.

removed: [functions]\nverify_jwt = true ← this installed tool version only understands per-function settings, not one shared setting for all functions; removing it is safe since "on" was already the default behavior with nothing else set.
Why not just tell the Founder to upgrade the CLI instead?

Modified cron-hard-delete, user-delete, user-export (edge functions)
▾
What this does
These three server functions handle a user's legal right to delete their account or download their own data — plus the background job that permanently erases a deleted account's data after 72 hours. This session deployed the versions of them that read/write the current tables instead of the old, soon-to-be-removed ones.
Input → Output
Input
A signed-in user's request to export or delete their account; or the scheduled job's own trigger
→
Output
A download link for export; a confirmation + deletion timeline for delete; a count of accounts actually purged for the scheduled job
Flow through it
signed-in test account→ export → 202 queued → complete→ delete → 202 soft-deleted→ scheduled purge job → runs clean
Key line of code
supabase/functions/_shared/services/scheduler/hard-delete.ts:110-125 ← the actual erase step now deletes from the current tables (never_list, user preferences, etc.) instead of the old, soon-to-be-removed schema.
Why deploy before removing the old schema, not after?
If the old schema were removed first, these three functions would start erroring immediately in production (they'd try to read tables that no longer exist) — deploy-then-remove is the only safe order, and the removal step itself refuses to run until the new tables exist.

Modified ops/quality/ui/run_ui.mjs
▾
What this does
A headless-browser script that opens the web build of the app and takes evidence (screenshot, console log, network log) for every screen. It used to visit only the home screen; it now reads the app's own screen folder and visits every screen that exists, so new screens get covered automatically.
Input → Output
Input
A running web address for the app (e.g. from `expo start --web`)
→
Output
One screenshot + console log + network log per screen, plus a pass/fail summary the quality report reads
Flow through it
reads mobile/app's screen folder→ builds the list of screen addresses→ visits each one in a headless browser→ saves a screenshot + logs per screen
Key line of code
for (const route of routes) { ... await page.screenshot(...) } ← loops over every discovered screen instead of one hardcoded screen
Why discover screens from the folder instead of a hardcoded list?
A hardcoded list silently goes stale — someone adds a new screen and forgets to add it here, so it never gets checked. Reading the app's own screen folder means the check always matches what's actually shipping.
What about screens that need a real ID in the URL (like a recipe page)?
A placeholder value is substituted (e.g. "sample-dish") so the screen is still reachable and screenshotted, even though it won't show real recipe data — that's enough to catch a broken/blank page.
DB Local practice database (Docker)
▾
What this does
A private copy of the database, running only on this machine, used to prove the quality report's database check without touching the real production database.
Input → Output
Input
The 48 schema-building files in database/migrations, run in order
→
Output
A working local database with 28 tables in the app's main schema — enough for the quality check to confirm "connected, correctly structured"
Flow through it
start local database (Docker)→ run all 48 schema files in order→ quality report connects and counts tables
Key line of code
select count(*) from information_schema.tables where table_schema='ghar_re' ← the exact check the quality report runs to prove the database is real and structured
Why not just point the check at the real production database?
The production database is live and holds real user data — running quality checks against it risks disruption for no benefit, since a fresh local copy proves the schema is correct just as well.
One migration step failed locally — was that a real problem?
No. That one step revokes a permission on a function that only exists in the real production database (it was installed there by hand, on purpose, and is documented as such in an earlier migration's own comment). It's expected to be missing in a fresh local copy and doesn't affect anything else.

A chat conversation raised "which dish list does the app actually recommend from?" as an open question. What this does
A household's allergies are packed into one number, one bit per allergen (2=dairy, 4=gluten, etc.). Fish and mustard were tagged in the underlying ingredient data but had no bit assigned, so selecting them was impossible and they were silently never excluded.

The engine's own allergy-exclusion logic already worked off plain allergen names read straight from ingredient data, not a fixed bit list — so once the bit existed and got decoded back to "fish"/"mustard", the engine could already act on it correctly.

⛔ Before this session

Mid-session, a concurrent WP-20/WP-21 cutover dropped the entire ghar_re schema from production (migration 050) — the exact table all of WP-19's research had been writing into — and its own audit confirmed no live code path had ever read that schema anyway.
→
✅ After this session
181 of 810 dishes now have cited aliases (352 rows) after six more research batches, and — critically — the entire alias ontology now lives on public.dish_name_synonyms, a new table FK'd to the real, live public.dishes (802 rows). All 352 previously-researched alias rows were migrated verbatim (same citations, same confidence scores) rather than re-researched, and the whole chain was re-tested end-to-end against the actual public.dishes seed data, not a stub loader.

10 files touched

1. Six more cited-alias batches (8-13), 99 dishes / 181 rows. Batch 8: Karnataka classics (Mysore Pak, Vangi Bath, Kesari Bath, Akki Rotti, Mangalorean Fish Gassi) plus Bengali cuisine (Machher Jhol, Shorshe Ilish, Aloo Posto, Luchi, Cholar Dal, Kosha Mangsho, Mishti Doi, Sandesh, Rasgulla, Begun Bhaja). Batch 9: more Bengal + Tulu Nadu (Chingri Malai Curry, Doi Maach, Shukto, Patishapta, Kori Rotti). Batch 10: Maharashtra/Gujarat (Vada Pav, Misal Pav, Thalipeeth, Bhakri, Sol Kadhi, Modak, Shrikhand, Khandvi, Thepla, Fafda Jalebi, Kombdi Vade, Ghugni). Batch 11: more Maharashtra/Gujarat (Sabudana Khichdi, Batata Vada, Amti, Dal Dhokli, Handvo, Patra, Basundi, Gathiya, Mohanthal, Khakhra, Methi Na Gota, Rotla). Batch 12: Goan cuisine (Vindaloo, Xacuti, Bebinca, Sorpotel, Fish Recheado, Prawn Balchao, Pao/Poi, Goan Fish Curry, Khichu, Muthiya). Batch 13: Rajasthani/Kashmiri/Andhra (Dal Baati Churma, Laal Maas, Gatte Ki Sabzi, Ker Sangri, Kashmiri Dum Aloo, Yakhni, Kahwa, Noon Chai, Gushtaba, Haak, Gongura Chicken, Gutti Vankaya). Same cited-research + safety-filter discipline throughout — several near-conflicts caught and excluded (e.g. "Solkadhi" vs "Sol Kadhi", "Goshtaba" vs "Gushtaba", "Zarda" already a separate catalogue dish).

2. Mid-push discovery: WP-19's entire target schema had been dropped. While merging batch 13 to main, found that a concurrent session had executed WP-21 (migration 050, certified in REPO-CERT-030): DROP SCHEMA ghar_re CASCADE against production, verified afterward with a direct psql query showing 0 rows in pg_namespace for that schema name. WP-21's own audit had independently confirmed no live code path ever read ghar_re.* to begin with — the real running recommendation engine reads from public.dishes and a build-time JSON bundle instead. That meant all 13 WP-19 batches (352 alias rows) had been researching real, correctly-cited data into a table that was both physically gone and never actually wired to production. Stopped adding more batches immediately rather than continuing onto a dead target or silently discarding 13 batches of real research, and asked the Founder how to proceed.

3. Retargeted onto public.dishes — content preserved, only the target fixed. Founder's direction: redirect to public.dishes. Built migration 051 (public.dish_name_synonyms, FK'd ON DELETE CASCADE to the real live public.dishes, the same "real aliases need a source_url" check constraint and public-read RLS policy pattern public.dishes itself already uses) and its rollback. Built validation 909 as a direct adaptation of the retired validation 907 (columns exist, every 'real' alias has source_url+confidence, alias_type is a valid kind, no orphan dish_id) plus one new structural check: no alias string may equal a *different* dish's own canonical name in public.dishes — the safety filter WP-19 has applied by hand since batch 1, now also enforced by the database itself. Then wrote a Python script that mechanically parsed all 13 old seed files (122-134) and re-emitted every one of the 352 alias rows against the new table — identical synonym, alias_type, region, language, source_url, and confidence for every row; the only thing that changed is how dish_id is resolved (SELECT id FROM public.dishes WHERE name = '...' instead of the retired deterministic md5('ghar_re.dish:'||name) scheme). No alias was re-researched, re-worded, or re-scored.

4. Tested against the REAL public.dishes this time, not a stub loader. Every prior WP-19 batch's local test used an uncommitted stub loader to simulate the full 810-dish catalogue in ghar_re.dishes, because the real DB only ever had a 39-dish golden sample there. This time, testing needed no such workaround: public.dishes already has its own real seed (106_seed_dishes.sql, 802 rows, deployed to production per earlier work packages), so the test ran migration 051 → seeds 105 (cuisines) + 106 (dishes) → seed 135 (aliases) → validation 909 against genuinely real data. All four validation checks passed; re-running seed 135 a second time inserted 0 new rows (idempotent). 348 of the 352 migrated rows actually loaded — the remaining 4 (for "Dal Baati Churma" and "Sadya Thali") resolved to zero matching rows because those 2 exact names aren't present in the 802-row public.dishes, a pre-existing gap against the 810-dish catalogue.json the service bundle uses, surfaced here but not this session's to fix.

5. What's still pending. 181 of 810 dishes have cited aliases (352 rows); 629 remain — a realistic multi-session undertaking, as flagged in prior sessions. The 802-vs-810 public.dishes/catalogue.json naming gap is now a known, surfaced issue for a future WP. The classify_dishes.py → catalogue.json synonym-export gap (logged since S51) is unaffected by this session's retarget and remains open.

S61 · Recommendation Engine Phase 3 (final phase) — s_pref stub, ModelArtifactProvider, training pipeline
Closed the last gap in the 4-phase RE build: the master scoring formula's `+ w_pref·S_pref` term now exists as a real, registry-wired ScoringModule instead of only a docstring comment — but it is deliberately UNFIT, contributing exactly 0.0 to every live score, since no real training data or trained model exists yet. Also built (but never ran against real data) the offline training pipeline that will one day produce that model.
⛔ Before this session
Phases 0-2 (feedback plumbing, ScoringModule registry, epsilon-greedy exploration) were done. No `S_pref` term existed anywhere in code — only in a comment inside score()'s docstring. There was no seam for injecting a trained preference model, and no code at all for turning real feedback_events into a trained artifact.
→
✅ After this session
`s_pref` is a registered ScoringModule (phase="pref") that every request's score() call now genuinely includes — but it returns exactly 0.0 (checked two independent ways: the module's own enabled/artifact checks, AND its weight defaulting to 0.0) so nothing about any household's recommendations changed. Golden-master stayed byte-identical, zero diff, no --update. A `ModelArtifactProvider` seam (mirroring the existing Config injection pattern) and a fixture-tested offline training pipeline now exist for a future session to actually use once real feedback data exists — neither was run against real production data, since there is none yet.

What was built this session
Aug 3, 2026
17 files touched

1. s_pref — a real ScoringModule that is deliberately unfit. ghar_re_core/preference.py's s_pref(dish, theta, ctx) returns exactly 0.0 whenever `pref_model.yaml`'s `enabled` flag is off (the state today) OR no trained artifact is loaded (also true today, unconditionally) — either check alone is sufficient. It is registered into modules_default.DEFAULT_REGISTRY as `phase="pref"`, with its weight (`CONFIG.w_pref`) *also* defaulting to 0.0 as a second, independent safety net. Nothing is fit, nothing is fabricated — the slot in the master formula simply exists in code now instead of only in a docstring comment.

2. Proved phase="pref" can never leak into existing scoring. The single biggest risk this phase carried: registering a new module in the shared registry could silently change every household's score. base() and the cohort term in score() each call `DEFAULT_REGISTRY.combine(...)` with an EXPLICIT phase filter ("base"/"cohort"), never "all phases" — so `s_pref` never reaches them. `score()` now also adds its own separate, explicit `combine(..., phase="pref")` call for the `+ w_pref·S_pref` term, which is unconditionally 0.0 today. Golden-master (`pytest ghar_re_core/tests/test_golden_master.py`) ran before and after this work: byte-identical, zero diff, no `--update` used — proving score-neutrality by actual test, not by inspection alone.

3. ModelArtifactProvider — the seam for a future trained model. ghar_re_core/model_provider.py mirrors the existing `Config`/`CONFIG` injection pattern exactly: `active_model()`/`set_active_model()`/a `PREF_MODEL` proxy. `NullModelArtifactProvider` (no artifact, ever) is the only provider actually constructed anywhere in this repo right now. `FileModelArtifactProvider(path)` is built (loads a joblib file, returns `None` gracefully if the path doesn't exist) but nothing calls it with a real path — activating it later is meant to be a config change (point `pref_model.yaml.model_artifact_path` at a real file + flip `enabled: true`), not a code change.

4. Feature extraction — one function, shared by inference and training. ghar_re_core/features.py's `extract_features(dish, theta, ctx)` concatenates household/context fields (diet, region, slot, season, weekday, interaction_count, plus `household_type` as an honest proxy for "household size" since no literal member-count field exists in theta) with every OTHER registered module's raw score value — deliberately skipping `phase="pref"` itself to avoid s_pref recursively calling its own feature extractor once a real model exists.

5. Training pipeline — built, fixture-tested, never run on real data. New `ghar_re_core/training/` package (nested under the existing `ghar_re_core` package, not a new top-level folder — no RACR needed, matches the plan's own suggested placement exactly). `dataset.py` loads an offline feedback-export JSONL (never queries Postgres directly — that boundary stays with Edge Functions), filters to `data_source == "real"` only, excludes ambiguous `shown_not_tapped`/`edit`/`swap` rows from labeling (never labelled 0, per the no-fabricated-labels rule), and labels `accept`/`like` as 1 and `dislike` as 0. A guard (`guard_sufficient_data`) refuses to fit — raising, writing nothing — if there are zero real labeled rows or only one label class present (a single-class fit would silently produce a meaningless constant model). `train_pref_model.py` is a runnable CLI (`python -m ghar_re_core.training.train_pref_model --feedback-export --out `) that vectorizes features, fits a small `sklearn.LogisticRegression`, and writes a joblib artifact + a holdout AUC/accuracy/coefficient eval report. `scikit-learn`/`joblib` were added as a new `training` optional-dependency extra in `pyproject.toml` — nothing in the live scoring path needs them, only running this pipeline does. This script has NEVER been run against real production feedback_events (0 rows exist today) — only against small, clearly-synthetic fixture rows in tests, proving the pipeline mechanics work without pretending any model is trained.

6. Bundle regeneration. `ghar_re_service`'s baked config bundle loads every file `Config.__init__` loads, including the new `pref_model.yaml` — missed this once (caught by running the full `ghar_re_service/tests/` suite, which failed with `FileNotFoundError`), added `pref_model.yaml` to `export_bundle.py`'s `CONFIG_FILES` allow-list, and re-ran the exporter to regenerate `ghar_re_service/data/bundle/config/pref_model.yaml` + `manifest.json`.

7. Verification. `pytest ghar_re_core/tests/test_golden_master.py -v` — 1 passed, byte-identical, zero diff, no `--update`. `pytest ghar_re_core/tests/` — 83 passed. `pytest ghar_re_service/tests/` — 68 passed. One existing Phase-1 test (`test_registry_module_names_match_expected_set`) had its assertion updated from "phase=pref is empty" to "phase=pref contains exactly s_pref" — an intentional, expected update to reflect Phase 3 legitimately registering the module, not a scoring-math change.

S63 · Dish-pick calibration grid — 3 meal slots × 5 dishes, mixing good matches with deliberate mismatches
Replaced the post-onboarding flat like-list with a smarter 3×5 grid (breakfast/lunch/dinner, 5 dishes each) that quietly mixes 3 dishes the engine genuinely thinks fit with 2 dishes that are still 100% safe to eat but a deliberately weak personal match — so an early "like" tap on a mismatch is a cheap, strong signal for correcting someone's taste profile sooner.
⛔ Before this session
The post-onboarding taste-calibration screen was a flat scrolling list of 15 dishes, all of them the engine's own top guesses — liking one only ever confirmed what the engine already believed, never corrected it.
→
✅ After this session
The same screen now shows a 3×5 grid — Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner columns, 5 dish cards each — where 2 of the 5 per slot are deliberately weak-fit (but still safe/diet-eligible) dishes. Liking one of those is a much stronger, earlier correction signal. Which 2 those are is never shown or guessable in the UI.

Newghar_re_core/calibration.py
▾
What this does
Exports calibration_grid(household, catalogue=None, weekday="Monday", household_id=None, n_positive=3, n_negative=2). For each of breakfast/lunch/dinner it ranks every slot-eligible dish by the existing engine score, picks the top-3 diverse-by-class/cuisine dishes as expected_positive, and separately picks 2 low-scoring diverse dishes (still eligible/safe, excluding any cuisine/class a positive already used) as planted_negative.
Input → Output
Input
A household's derived profile + the dish catalogue (same inputs meal_planner.py already uses)
→
Output
A dict of 3 slots, each holding 5 dish cells tagged expected_positive/planted_negative, cell order shuffled per household+slot
Flow through it
_ranked_eligible() scores every slot-eligible dish→_pick_positives() top-3 diverse→_pick_negatives() bottom-2 diverse, excluding positives' class/cuisine→shuffle cell order (seeded)
Key line of code
out.append((S.score(d, theta, ctx, objective), d)) ← _ranked_eligible() reuses scoring.py's own score() call unchanged; calibration.py never computes a score itself
Why is this a new file instead of a function inside meal_planner.py?
Founder required the RE core's actual scoring/eligibility/derivation math to stay untouched this session. A brand-new additive file that only calls existing public functions — mirroring meal_planner.py's own established charter — satisfies that while still building the feature; extending meal_planner.py would have meant editing an existing WP-18 core file rather than adding alongside it.
Why does _pick_negatives() exclude any cuisine/class already used by a positive?
Without that exclusion a "mismatch" dish could accidentally share a cuisine or class with a genuine top pick, diluting the calibration signal — the two roles need to feel genuinely distinct to the household, not just differently scored.

▾
What this does
4 tests covering calibration_grid(): correct grid shape and role-counts per slot, every returned dish (positive AND negative) independently passes scoring.eligible, deterministic dish selection with no household_id, and that a household_id only reorders cells, never changes which dishes get picked.

→
Output

python -m pytest ghar_re_core/tests/test_calibration.py -q ← all 4 pass on their own; run alongside test_meal_planner.py (13 passed total) to confirm no interference with the sibling WP-18 planner module
Why specifically assert every negative dish passes scoring.eligible, not just that it exists?
The entire safety promise of "planted_negative but still safe" rests on that one guarantee — a test that only checked count/shape could pass even if a negative dish accidentally violated an allergen or diet rule. The test asserts eligibility independently for every cell, positive or negative.

Why does the Finish button always continue to /weekly-plan regardless of selection count?
This screen's job is calibration signal collection, not a hard gate — forcing a minimum number of likes before continuing would add onboarding friction for no correctness reason; a household that likes nothing still needs its weekly plan.
Was the navigation graph changed at all?
No — same route (/cold-start), same entry point (onboarding step-5's router.replace), same exit point (router.push to /weekly-plan). Only what renders inside the screen changed.

Visually verify the grid in a simulator/browser; the other concurrent session's pairing.py and onboarding step-1..4/OnboardingChips.tsx work is out of scope here and should be reviewed on its own.
S64 · Closed the feedback loop, made DPDP rights reachable, real error alerting
Fixed a bug where household activity was never actually being recorded, gave users a way to react to and understand their meal recommendations, put the already-built "export my data / delete my account" tools somewhere a user can actually find them, and made sure a real error in production now reaches an alert instead of just a log file.
⛔ Before this session
A like/dislike tap on the Home tab had nothing to attach to, so it silently did nothing. Editing your diet or allergens after onboarding looked like it saved but actually changed nothing in the database. The app had no history view, no profile-edit screen, and no way to reach the already-built data export/account deletion tools at all. Production errors only ever showed up in a log nobody was watching.
→
Liking or disliking a meal on the Home tab now records against that recommendation, with a "Why this?" toggle showing the match reason. A new History tab shows your past recommendations. A new Profile-edit screen actually saves diet/allergen changes. A new Settings tab lets you request a data export or delete your account. Every planning call now correctly records which household made it. A production error now reaches a configurable webhook alert, not just a log line.

Modifiedmobile/app/(tabs)/today.tsx — DishCard
▾
What this does
Each meal shown on the Home tab is now its own card with a like/dislike button and a "Why this?" toggle. Tapping like or dislike posts feedback tied to the specific recommendation that produced this dish; tapping "Why this?" reveals the match score and cuisine/class reasoning already present on the dish data.
Input → Output
Input
A tap on 👍/👎 or "Why this?", plus the dish's request_id from the plan the screen already loaded
→
Output
A POST to /v1/feedback recorded against that request_id, or an expanded explanation panel
Flow through it
User taps like/dislike→ postFeedback()→ POST /v1/feedback→ resolves against recommendation_events
Key line of code
return postFeedback({ request_id: requestId, event_type: eventType, dish_name: dish.name }); ← the whole feedback tap in one call, using the request_id the plan/handler.ts fix (P0-4) now guarantees exists for this surface
Why did feedback taps on Home not work before this session?
meal_plan and class_dishes — the surfaces the Home tab actually calls — weren't in the server's FEEDBACK_ELIGIBLE_SURFACES set, so no recommendation_events row ever existed for feedback to resolve against. The tap itself wasn't broken; there was simply nothing on the server side for it to attach to.
Newmobile/app/history.tsx
▾
What this does
A new screen listing the caller's own past recommendations, most recent first, with a plain-English label for each outcome (Served, Timed out, Failed, Unavailable) instead of raw status codes.
Input → Output
Input
The signed-in user opening the History tab
→
Output
A scrollable, human-readable list of that household's recommendation_events rows
Flow through it
History tab mounts→ fetchHistory()→ plan surface:"history"→ fetchRecentRecommendationEvents()
Key line of code
const OUTCOME_LABEL: Record<string, string> = { success: "Served", partial: "Served (partial)", ... } ← translates internal outcome codes into words a non-technical user recognizes
Why route this through the plan function instead of querying the database directly from the app?
Every other surface already goes through plan/handler.ts for auth and household-ownership checks (requireOwnership) — reusing that path means History gets the same security guarantee for free instead of the app needing its own direct-to-database read path.
Newmobile/app/profile-edit.tsx
▾
What this does
Lets a user change their diet type and allergen selections after onboarding. Pre-fills from their current saved profile, then saves through the same write path onboarding itself uses.
Input → Output
Input
Chip selections for diet type and allergens
→
Output
An updated profiles row, this time actually saved (see the P1-4 database fix below)
Flow through it
fetchProfile() pre-fills the form→ user edits chips→ postHousehold()→ buildProfilePatch/updateProfileFields
Key line of code
import { allergenFlags } from "@/onboarding/toHouseholdWrite"; ← reuses onboarding's own allergen bit-mapping instead of re-deriving it, so the two flows can never quietly drift apart
Why was this worth building this session specifically?
Without the paired store.ts fix, this screen would have looked fully functional while silently discarding every edit — building the screen surfaced the bug, and fixing the bug is what makes the screen honest.
Newmobile/app/(tabs)/settings.tsx
▾
What this does
The first reachable UI for the DPDP data-subject-rights endpoints — requesting an export of your data, or deleting your account. Also links out to Profile-edit and History. Both backend endpoints already existed and were already authorized; neither had anywhere in the app to be triggered from before this screen.
Input → Output
Input
A tap on "Export my data," or the exact phrase "DELETE MY ACCOUNT" typed to confirm deletion
→
Output
An export job kicked off and polled, or the account actually deleted
Flow through it
Settings tab→ requestExport()/deleteAccount()→ GET /v1/user/export or POST /v1/user/delete
Key line of code
export const REQUIRED_CONFIRMATION_PHRASE = "DELETE MY ACCOUNT"; ← account deletion only fires if the typed text matches exactly, a deliberate friction point against accidental deletion
Why was this treated as a compliance gap rather than just a missing feature?
India's DPDP Act requires these rights be user-initiated. An endpoint that exists and is authorized but has no UI a user can reach isn't a satisfied right — it's an unreachable one, which is a real audit finding, not a nice-to-have.
Newmobile/src/api/account.ts
▾
What this does
The API client layer backing the Settings screen: requestExport(), pollExport() and deleteAccount(), each a thin call to an already-existing Edge Function.

→

function deleteAccount(userId: string, confirmationPhrase: string): Promise<DeleteAccountResponse> ← the confirmation phrase is required at the API layer too, not just enforced by the screen's UI
Why require the confirmation phrase in the client function's own signature?
So the safeguard travels with the function itself — any future screen that calls deleteAccount() has to supply a confirmation phrase by construction, rather than relying on every future caller to remember to add its own UI gate.

Modifiedhousehold_context (via plan/handler.ts, P0-1)
▾
What this does
Every planning surface with a resolved household now calls the existing recordHouseholdContext helper after a successful engine response — the helper always existed and worked, it was simply never called from the one function real traffic actually uses.
Input → Output
Input
A resolved household id, slot and weekday from a successful plan call
→
Output

Flow through it

Key line of code
if (resolvedHouseholdId) { await recordHouseholdContext(ctx, resolvedHouseholdId, { slot: body.slot, weekday: body.weekday }); } ← best-effort, guarded so it can never turn a successful plan response into a failure
Why had household_context stayed at exactly 0 rows despite 126+ served recommendations?
recommendations/handler.ts (which has zero live callers) was the only place that ever called recordHouseholdContext. plan/handler.ts — the function real traffic actually goes through — simply never called it. The writer worked fine; it was just never invoked from the path that matters.
Modifiedrecommendation_events (via plan/handler.ts, P0-4)
▾
What this does
FEEDBACK_ELIGIBLE_SURFACES widened from cold_start/calibration-only to also include meal_plan and class_dishes — the surfaces the actively-routed Home tab actually calls — so a like/dislike tap there has a recommendation_events row to resolve against.
Input → Output
Input
A successful meal_plan or class_dishes response with a resolved household
→
Output
A recommendation_events row keyed by request_id
Flow through it
plan handler serves meal_plan/class_dishes→ FEEDBACK_ELIGIBLE_SURFACES.has(surface)→ recordRecommendationEvent()
Key line of code
const FEEDBACK_ELIGIBLE_SURFACES = new Set(["cold_start", "calibration", "meal_plan", "class_dishes"]); ← weekly_plan/recipe stay deliberately excluded — one returns classes not scored dishes, the other isn't a recommendation at all
Why not just make every surface feedback-eligible?
weekly_plan returns classes, not individual scored dishes — there's nothing coherent for a like/dislike to attach to. recipe isn't a recommendation at all. Being explicit about which surfaces qualify avoids creating meaningless feedback rows.

▾
What this does
+buildProfilePatch()/updateProfileFields(): a repeat call to POST /v1/household with changed answers now updates the existing profiles row's fields, instead of silently doing nothing once the row already existed.
Input → Output
Input

→

household handler sees profile already exists→ buildProfilePatch(screens)→ updateProfileFields(ctx, profileId, patch)

export async function updateProfileFields(ctx, profileId, patch) ← the function that literally didn't exist before this session — every call after the first profile insert was previously a silent no-op
How was this bug found?
Building profile-edit.tsx required a real update path to test against — reading store.ts to wire the new screen surfaced that no such path existed at all.
Modifiedplan edge function — history/profile surfaces (P1-3, P1-4)
▾
What this does
Two new pure-read surfaces on POST /v1/plan: "history" calls the new fetchRecentRecommendationEvents(), "profile" calls the existing loadHouseholdRaw() — neither calls the recommendation engine at all.
Input → Output
Input
{surface: "history", limit?} or {surface: "profile"}
→
Output
A list of the caller's own recommendation_events rows, or their current composed household profile

authenticate + requireOwnership→ surface routing→ fetchRecentRecommendationEvents() or loadHouseholdRaw()

const events = await fetchRecentRecommendationEvents(ctx, householdIdForHistory, limit); ← read-only and fail-open, same auth/ownership guard as every scoring surface

requireOwnership already guarantees a caller only ever sees their own household's data — reusing it for reads costs nothing and rules out an entire class of "wrong household's history leaked" bugs by construction.
Modifiedhousehold/schema.ts — allergen_flags cap
▾
What this does
The profile envelope's allergen_flags validation cap, corrected from max(127) (the old frozen 7-bit allergen model) to max(511) (the live 9-bit model, per the WP-21 fish/mustard extension).
Input → Output
Input
An allergen_flags integer that includes the fish or mustard bit
→
Output
Accepted (previously rejected with a validation error)

Profile-edit sends allergenFlags()→ zod schema validates→ max(511) now accepts the full 9-bit range
Key line of code
allergen_flags: z.number().int().min(0).max(511), ← was max(127); note the separate per-member envelope's own cap is still max(127), not touched this session
Why wasn't the per-member allergen cap fixed too, if it has the same bug?
Flagged but left out of scope this session — the profile-edit screen only writes the top-level profile envelope, so fixing that cap was what the new screen actually needed. The member-envelope cap is a known follow-up, not silently missed.
New_shared/telemetry/telemetry.ts + error-boundary.ts (P1-7)
▾
What this does
+webhookSink()/resolveTelemetrySink(), wired into error-boundary.ts — the one place every Edge Function's uncaught error already passes through — so a real alerting channel is reachable across every function, not just plan/household.
Input → Output
Input
Any uncaught 500-level error in any Edge Function
→
Output
A POST to the configured TELEMETRY_WEBHOOK_URL, always also still logged
Flow through it
error-boundary catches an error→ resolveTelemetrySink(logger, webhookUrl)→ webhookSink POSTs, or falls back to log-only
Key line of code
resolveTelemetrySink(ctx.logger, ctx.config.telemetryWebhookUrl).captureError(e, {...}) ← picks webhookSink only when a URL is configured; never throws, so a failed webhook POST can never itself cause a 500
Is a real alert actually firing in production right now?
No — no real TELEMETRY_WEBHOOK_URL was provided this session, so production currently still falls back to log-only, same as before. The plumbing is real and tested; wiring in an actual Slack/PagerDuty/etc. URL later is a one-line env var change, not a code change.

S85 · Dish ingestion pipeline
Built the ETL that loads the 6,871-recipe CSV into the dish catalogue, with dedupe, ontology mapping, AI enrichment (mock mode), and image plumbing — schema written, dry-run validated on the real file, not yet applied to a live database.
⛔ Before this session
The Indian food dataset CSV sat unused in database/seeds/ — no code path loaded it into the dish catalogue, no dedupe/ontology/enrichment logic existed for it, and there was no way to track an import run, its per-row outcomes, or errors.
→
A dry-run-capable, batched, idempotent ETL exists that parses the real CSV, dedupes near-duplicate dish names, maps cuisine/course/diet to this repo's own ontology tables (no fabricated external API), infers missing tags/region with a heuristic fallback when no Groq key is set, and is ready to apply once a live database and migration 076 are in place.

A dish missing a photo now gets a real AI-generated one: an LLM fills in a fixed standardized prompt template, Pollinations.ai renders it, and the bytes go straight (no local disk write) into a signed Cloudinary upload named to match the existing ghar_re_service asset convention — gated by an idempotency check so a rerun never regenerates a dish that already has an image.

image_prompt.py owns a fixed, verbatim-ported prompt template (from the Founder-supplied xlsx, confirmed against 5 sample rows) and calls Groq (primary), Hugging Face Inference API (alternate), or a deterministic heuristic (last resort) to fill in only the 4 variable fields — never letting the model generate the template text itself. images.py ports the Founder's Pollinations reference script's generation mechanism (flux-pro, 1024x1024, retry/backoff) but drops its local-disk/CSV bookkeeping entirely: bytes go straight from the HTTP response into an in-memory, signed Cloudinary upload under a <dish_slug>_hero_01_<random> public_id matching ghar_re_service's existing convention exactly (verified: slugify("Thai Spring Roll (Fried)") == "thai_spring_roll_fried"). Idempotency is a dish-level guard (db.load_dish_ids_with_image), not just a table constraint. Executed and verified
`--dry-run` (with and without `--skip-images`) ran end to end against the real CSV with Stage 5 wired in, zero network calls, confirmed by sub-100ms elapsed time. `images.slugify()` and `image_prompt.assemble_prompt()`/heuristic fallback were unit-checked directly. `images.PollinationsClient.generate_png()` was called for real against the live host and reproduced a proxy 403 (Tunnel connection failed) — this is the real network-attempt evidence the task asked for.
Written but NOT executed
Every live-credential path: CloudinaryUploader.upload_png() signed upload, ImagePromptGenerator._call_groq()/_call_hf(). `env | grep -iE 'GROQ|HF_API|HUGGINGFACE|CLOUDINARY'` returned nothing — no credentials are configured in this environment, and the sandbox's outbound proxy independently blocks all three hosts (confirmed via $HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status's recentRelayFailures log) regardless of credentials. Migration 077's SQL and the `--apply` persistence path for images are unexecuted, same status as migration 076 from S85.

S87 · Governed synthetic training ingestion
Loaded both generated workbooks into private, versioned research staging while proving that no synthetic user, plan or event targets production.
⛔ Before this session
Training artifacts existed on disk, but there was no row-level database lineage, rejected-row store or approved way to load them without risking production-data contamination.
→
✅ After this session
Every workbook row can be retained with its exact source and validation outcome, while valid derived records go only to private synthetic staging through a deterministic, repeatable and confirmation-gated load.
